meta.client: VS Code users who work with databases · open source by BrianLab
meta.tagline: A free database client inside VS Code, with no cap on connections

overview.summary: Open DB Client is a free VS Code extension for working with databases, with no limit on how many connections you keep. One tree in the sidebar holds PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, SQLite, Redis and AWS Athena side by side: you browse tables, write and run queries, and edit the results in place. Passwords stay in the operating system's keychain, and an optional AI assistant writes and explains SQL using your own provider key.

users.name: Developer
users.goal: Keeps every database they work with in one sidebar, browses tables, runs queries and fixes rows without leaving the editor.

users.name: Data analyst on Athena
users.goal: Queries data in S3 through Athena and sees how many bytes each query scanned, because Athena bills by the byte.

users.name: Redis user
users.goal: Searches keys on the server, reads and edits values, and sets or clears expiry times.

users.name: Contributor
users.goal: Adds an engine, fixes a bug or ships a release, following the driver rule and the versioning policy.

loop: Add a connection. Its password goes to the keychain; everything else is kept by VS Code.
Expand it in the sidebar to reach databases, schemas and tables, or Redis keys.
Click a table to preview its rows, or open a query panel for that connection.
Write a query, with autocomplete or help from the AI assistant, and run it.
Edit cells or rows in the results grid and save; the change is written back to the database.
Export the results, or save the query as a file in the tree to run again later.

components.name: Connection manager
components.summary: Owns every open connection and its SSH tunnel, connects on demand, and can tear everything down, including a connect that is stuck.
components.detail: ConnectionManager keeps three maps: live drivers, tunnels, and pending (in-flight) connects. getDriver(id) returns a live driver or builds one: it registers a Pending entry first, opens the SSH tunnel (capped at 15 s by withTimeout) for non-SQLite connections with SSH on, creates the driver via the registry, fetches secrets from the store and calls driver.connect(secrets). On failure it logs, disposes what it built and rethrows. disposeAll() (Stop All, Reset, deactivate) disposes live and pending drivers and closes every tunnel with allSettled / try-catch so one failure cannot leave the rest running. src/timeout.ts is the dependency-free withTimeout helper shared with the tree.

components.name: SSH tunnel
components.summary: Opens an SSH connection to a jump host and forwards a local port to the real database, so the driver connects to this machine as if the database were local.
components.detail: openTunnelForConfig() resolves the target host/port from the fields or, for connection-string connections, by parsing the URL (csTarget), opens an SshTunnel and returns an effective config rewritten to 127.0.0.1:<local port> (csRewriteHostPort for strings, keeping user/password/db/query). SshTunnel uses ssh2: buildConnectConfig() honours Auto/Password/Key/Agent; with Auto it offers SSH_AUTH_SOCK, an explicit key or the first default ~/.ssh key that parses with the given passphrase, then the password. readyTimeout is the per-connection SSH timeout (default 5000 ms). A net server on 127.0.0.1:0 forwards each socket with forwardOut().
responsibilities: Work out the real database host/port, including from a connection string.

components.summary: Builds and reads connection export files: the passwordless default, the passphrase-encrypted file, and the plain-text one; plus the connection-string helpers.

components.name: Driver contract and registry
components.summary: The one interface every database engine implements, plus the switch that picks an engine for a connection.
components.detail: `Driver.ts` defines `Driver` (connect, children, query, previewTable, getDDL, updateCell/deleteRow/insertRow, schemaHints) and the data shapes that cross it: `QueryResult` (the single contract from any driver to the grid, with optional engine extras such as `ttl`, `bytesScanned`, `page`, `editable`), `TreeItemData` (one tree child with an opaque `path`) and `ConnectSecrets` (secrets are handed in by the host; a driver never touches SecretStorage). components.name: PostgreSQL driver
components.summary: Talks to PostgreSQL through a pure-JavaScript client, with one lazy pool per database so the whole server can be browsed.
components.detail: Tree shape: connection → Security (users/roles) + every non-template database (from `pg_database`, including ones the role cannot enter, marked `no connect`) → schemas → tables/views → Columns/Indexes/Foreign Keys/Triggers folders (`tableFolders`, sentinel path segments like `@columns`). Keeps a `Pool` per database (max 4) and rewrites the database segment of a connection string per pool (M5.5). `query()` checks out a client explicitly so it can record the backend PID; `cancel()` sends `pg_cancel_backend` on a second connection, so `canCancel = true`. Previews are `SELECT * ... LIMIT/OFFSET` with quoted identifiers and parameterized filter values (`ILIKE`), plus a `count(*)` for the pager. `getDDL` is reconstructed from information_schema and labelled approximate. Also exports `displaySql` and `tableFolders`, which the MySQL and SQLite drivers reuse.
responsibilities: List databases, schemas, tables, columns, indexes, foreign keys, triggers and roles
Run statements with real server-side cancellation
Preview tables with paging, sort, filters and primary-key editing
Reconstruct approximate DDL
Offer row editing on hand-typed single-table SELECTs

dependsOn.why: Implements the Driver interface.

components.name: MySQL / MariaDB driver
components.summary: Talks to MySQL and MariaDB through a pure-JavaScript client; the tree goes straight from databases to tables.
components.detail: Tree shape: connection → databases (information_schema.schemata minus system schemas) → tables/views → the same four folders as Postgres. One pool (connectionLimit 4). `query()` checks out a connection to learn its `threadId`; `cancel()` runs `KILL QUERY <id>` on another pooled connection, which ends the statement but not the session. Identifiers use backtick quoting (`quoteBacktick`). `getDDL` is the server's own `SHOW CREATE TABLE`. Note: `query()` ignores its `database` argument (`_database`), so a panel opened on one database runs against the connection's configured default unless the SQL is qualified. Imports `displaySql`/`tableFolders` from the Postgres driver.
responsibilities: List databases, tables, columns, indexes, foreign keys and triggers

components.name: SQLite driver (sql.js WASM)
components.summary: Opens a SQLite file by loading the whole thing into memory with the WebAssembly build of SQLite, and writes the whole file back after changes.
components.detail: `connect()` reads the file with `fs.readFileSync` into a `sql.js` `Database` (WASM located via `setSqliteWasmDir`, set at activation to `dist/`, where the bundle copies `sql-wasm.wasm`). Tree: connection → tables/views directly (single file = single database) → the four folders via PRAGMAs. `query()` runs `exec()` synchronously on the extension-host thread; any statement not starting with `select` triggers `persist()`, which `export()`s the whole database and overwrites the file. Grid edits (`updateCell`/`deleteRow`/`insertRow`) persist the same way. No `cancel()` on purpose: while sql.js runs nothing else on the host can, so an Abort could never be delivered. `getDDL` is the stored `sqlite_master.sql`. Note: `foreignKeys()` interpolates the table name into `PRAGMA foreign_key_list("...")` without `quoteIdent` (line 297), unlike every other site in the file.
responsibilities: Load a SQLite file into memory through WebAssembly
List tables, views, columns, indexes, foreign keys and triggers

components.name: Redis driver
components.summary: Talks to Redis: numbered databases, a server-side key search capped at 500 keys, typed value previews, element editing and TTLs.
components.detail: Tree: connection → `db0..dbN` (count from `CONFIG GET databases`, falling back to 16; key counts from `INFO keyspace`; only non-empty dbs plus the configured one) → keys. `scanKeys` walks `SCAN cursor [MATCH pattern] COUNT 500` until `KEY_LIMIT` (500) or a round-trip budget (20 unfiltered, 200 filtered) and reports `truncated`; keys are sorted and get one pipelined `PTTL` batch. `scanPattern` turns a plain search term into `*term*` and passes glob syntax through. `previewTable` reads `TYPE`, shapes the value so one element is addressable (string→value, list→index/value, hash→field/value, set→member, zset→member/score; lists and zsets capped at 200 with a `previewNotice`), attaches `ttl` and an `editable` pk column. `updateCell` preserves TTL on string edits; `deleteRow` with no pk deletes the whole key, with a pk only the element; `setTtl` runs `PEXPIRE` or `PERSIST`. `query()` tokenizes a command line and sends it via `call()`. `canCancel = false`: `cancel()` only stops waiting. Exports `KEY_FILTER_NODE`, which the tree imports.
responsibilities: List numbered databases with key counts
Search keys server-side with SCAN MATCH, capped and honest about truncation
Preview a key as a typed, editable grid with its TTL
Edit, add and delete elements; delete a whole key
Set or clear a key's expiry

dependsOn.why: Implements the Driver interface, including the optional setTtl.

components.name: AWS Athena driver
components.summary: Runs Athena queries through the AWS SDK and browses the Glue catalog through metadata APIs, built around the fact that every query costs money.
components.detail: Not a socket: `connect()` builds an `AthenaClient` with a credential provider (`profile` via `fromNodeProviderChain`, static `keys`, or the default chain) and makes one free `GetWorkGroup` call that proves credentials and reads the effective output location (a workgroup that enforces its own wins). Tree: catalog (folder) → database → table/view (view detected from `Parameters.table_type`) → columns, partition keys flagged; all from `ListDataCatalogs`/`ListDatabases`/`ListTableMetadata`/`GetTableMetadata`, never `information_schema` (that would be billed DML). Table lists cap at 300 with a visible truncation row; the tree filter is passed to Glue as `Expression`. `query()` = `StartQueryExecution` → poll `GetQueryExecution` (200 ms doubling to 1 s) → walk `GetQueryResults` pages (999 data rows each; header row detected, not assumed) up to 10,000 rows, then reports `bytesScanned`. Failed/cancelled runs report bytes scanned in the error. `cancel()` = `StopQueryExecution` (`canCancel = true`); `dispose()` deliberately does not cancel. No `countRows`, no editing, `getDDL` reconstructed with Hive backtick quoting and labelled approximate.
responsibilities: Resolve AWS credentials and validate the workgroup
Browse catalogs, databases, tables and columns with free metadata calls
Start, poll, cancel and page through query executions
Report bytes scanned on success, failure and cancel
Preview a table with one bounded statement and no server-side paging

dependsOn.why: Implements Driver and omits the optional row count on purpose.

components.name: Driver helpers
components.summary: Small shared pieces every SQL driver uses: identifier quoting, TLS options and completion-hint grouping.
components.detail: `ident.ts`: `quoteIdent` (double quotes, Postgres/SQLite) and `quoteBacktick` (MySQL) double the embedded quote character so a schema/table/column name can never break out of its identifier; values always travel as parameters. `displayIdent`/`displayBacktick`/`sqlLiteral` make readable display SQL only. `parseFromTable` best-effort extracts the table of a plain single-table SELECT so hand-typed queries can be edited, returning undefined for joins, unions, subqueries or multiple statements. `ssl.ts#buildTls` builds TLS options with verification on unless the user ticked allow-self-signed, loading CA/cert/key files. `hints.ts` holds the completion caps (2,000 tables, 20,000 columns; drivers fetch limit+1 to prove truncation) and `groupColumns`. Athena keeps its own Trino (`q`) and Hive (`qDdl`) quoters inside its driver.

Build display-only SQL text and literals

components.name: Query panel
components.summary: The editor and results grid where people type SQL or Redis commands, run them, and read, edit, filter, export and inspect the rows that come back.
components.detail: One webview per invocation (`QueryPanel`), built by `render()` as a single self-contained HTML string: inline CSS plus one nonce'd inline `<script>` under a strict CSP (`default-src 'none'; style-src 'unsafe-inline'; script-src 'nonce-…'`). No external loads, no modules: the pure webview helpers (`jsonView.ts`, `columnView.ts`) are shipped as `String.raw` source strings and concatenated into the script, because the production build minifies and `Function.prototype.toString()` injection would break only in the packaged extension. Host and webview talk only by message: the webview calls `vscode.postMessage({ type })`, dispatched by the `switch` in `onDidReceiveMessage` to a `handle*` host method that calls the `Driver` (`run`, `abort`, `page`, `refresh`, `sort`, `filter`, `update`, `delete`, `insert`, `setTtl`, `openRelated`, `export`, `copy`, `saveFile`, `format`, `complete`, `ai`, `aiReset`, `aiComplete`); the host answers with `this.post({ type })` (`result`, `error`, `aborted`, `abortCaps`, `status`, `updateResult`, `saved`, `setSql`, `context`, `completions`, `aiEnabled`/`aiDisabled`, `aiResult`, `aiCompletions`). Anything needing a native VS Code prompt (delete confirm, TTL input box, save dialog, large-copy confirm) is routed through the host. Out-of-order replies are dropped by sequence numbers (`reqSeq` for preview paging/sort/filter, `runSeq` for hand-typed runs, `acSeq` for completion). The file is ~2,500 lines; the host half is the top ~800 lines and the rest is the HTML/CSS/JS template. `exportView.ts` holds the host-side, unit-tested export projection and CSV writer. `miniMarkdown.ts` is listed here but is only imported by the settings panel.
responsibilities: SQL / command editor with highlight-to-run, Ctrl/Cmd+/ line comments (not on Redis), Format (dialect-aware, hidden on Redis) and in-panel autocomplete.

Run/abort state machine: one query in flight per panel, braille spinner on the Run button armed after 150 ms, Abort shown only when the driver has `cancel()`, labelled Stop waiting when `canCancel` is false, late results dropped by `runSeq`.

Results grid: typed headers with PK/FK/not-null markers, row-number gutter, client-side or server-backed sort and per-column filters, page-local global search, 100-row paging for previews, a 2,000-row paint cap with an honest scope note.
Inline editing on editable results: cell edit, Edit Data modal, + Row form, checked-row delete with modal confirm, Redis TTL edit/persist.

JSON viewer (summary chip, lazy tree with a 1,000-child cap, Raw tab for editing) and the Columns picker.

components.name: SQL language suite
components.summary: Works out which tables, columns, keywords and functions fit where the caret is, formats SQL in the connection's dialect, and gives saved query files suggestions and a Run lens.
components.detail: Three files. `sqlComplete.ts` is pure, VS Code-free completion reasoning: a backward token scan (not a grammar) that strips comments and strings, scopes to the current `;`-separated statement, resolves aliases (`aliasMap`, `tablesInScope`), classifies the caret position (`completionContext`: table / column / any, plus `expressionStart` after ORDER/GROUP/PARTITION BY and a `qualifier` after `x.`), and ranks exact > prefix > contains with kind tiers (`rank`, `suggest`). `sqlDialect.ts` is the only importer of `sql-formatter`, imported per dialect through `formatDialect` (postgres → postgresql, mysql, sqlite, athena → trino); it supplies `vocabularyFor(type)` for completion, `canFormat` (false for Redis) and `formatSql` with `keywordCase: "upper"`. `sqlFeatures.ts` registers VS Code-native providers for `{ language: "sql", scheme: "file" }`: a CompletionItemProvider (same `suggest`, capped at 400 items), a DocumentFormattingEditProvider, and a CodeLensProvider that puts ▶ Run / { } JSON on each `;`-split statement of a saved query file bound to a connection (`bindQueryDoc` map, with `QueryStore.resolveUri` as fallback). Unit-tested in `test/sqlComplete.test.js` and `test/sqlDialect.test.js`.
responsibilities: Context-aware, alias-aware, dialect-aware completion candidates for both the query panel and saved .sql files.
Withholding keywords where only an expression can start, so accepting the first suggestion cannot build ORDER BY DESC.
Dialect vocabulary from sql-formatter's tokenizer tables; a small static command list for Redis.
Formatting that throws on a parse error so callers leave the user's text untouched.
Native IntelliSense, Format Document and ▶ Run / { } JSON CodeLens for saved query files.

dependsOn.why: Maps a saved .sql file back to its connection and database when the in-memory binding is missing.
The native .sql completion fetches schema hints through the connection manager (which connects if needed) and caches them per connection and database.
Consumes the SchemaHints shape (tables, columns, columnsByTable, truncated).
The Run and JSON lenses invoke the runSql / runSqlJson commands.
Registers language providers with VS Code's own editor.

components.name: Saved queries
components.summary: Keeps saved queries as ordinary .sql files and folders in the extension's own storage, grouped by connection and database.
components.detail: `QueryStore` manages real files under `<globalStorageUri>/queries/<connId>@@<db>[@<schema>]/<folders…>/<name>.sql`, so VS Code's own editor does editing, saving and undo. `queryKey.ts` (pure, unit-tested in `test/queryStore.test.js`) encodes and parses the self-describing folder key; `resolveUri` parses it back to `{ connId, database }` for files opened without an in-memory binding. Every name segment is sanitised to `[\w.@-]` (anything else becomes `_`). `list` returns folders first then `.sql` files, each sorted; `createFile` writes a `-- <name>` header; `delete` is recursive with `useTrash: false`; `deleteAll` wipes the whole `queries` folder for Reset All Data. The tree's Query node and the newQueryFile / newQueryFolder / openQueryFile / runQueryFile / delete* commands in `extension.ts` are the callers.
responsibilities: Create, list, read and delete saved query files and folders per connection and database scope.
Map a file path back to the connection and database it belongs to.
Remove every saved query on Reset All Data.

dependsOn.why: Files live under the extension's globalStorageUri and are read and written through workspace.fs.

components.name: AI assistant service
components.summary: Runs Generate, Explain and Fix: checks the opt-out and consent, builds the schema context, calls the provider and records the cost.
components.detail: Host-side orchestration for the three assist verbs, kept out of queryPanel.ts so the panel only does message plumbing. `AiService.run` refuses a connection the user switched AI off for, asks for first-use consent (skipped for localhost endpoints), reads `schemaHints` and best-effort `foreignKeys` from the live driver, renders a compact schema bounded by a 6,000-token budget (`context.ts`), pins the dialect in the system prompt (`prompts.ts`), calls the provider and records exact token counts. It also owns the price-table operations behind Settings: listing models with prices, adding and refreshing rows, auto-pricing a model the first time it is used, and downloading the LiteLLM price list. A module-level `onDidChangeAiSettings` event tells every open query panel when AI settings change.
responsibilities: Gate every request on the per-connection opt-out and the one-time consent modal.
Build the schema context: full schema plus foreign keys when it fits, otherwise the tables the request names plus one foreign-key hop, and say it was trimmed.
Pin the engine dialect and the house rules (one fenced statement, no bind parameters, no destructive SQL unless asked) in each prompt.
Extract the SQL from the reply and tag destructive shapes and writes.
Record each call in the usage ledger and file a price row the first time a model is used.
Fetch model lists, provider prices and the LiteLLM price list for the Settings price table.
Broadcast AI settings changes so open panels show or hide the assist bar.

dependsOn.why: Reads the active provider, the stored key, consent and the per-connection opt-out.
Hands the finished prompt to whichever adapter the provider kind selects.
Records each call and reads the price table for the per-call estimate.
Schema context comes from the connection's own schema hints and foreign keys.
Shows the native consent modal and fires the settings-changed event.
Downloads the LiteLLM price list from GitHub directly.

components.name: AI provider adapters
components.summary: Two small hand-written adapters, Anthropic and OpenAI-compatible, behind one provider interface; presets are data.
components.detail: Mirrors the `Driver` architecture: callers use `AiProvider` only (`complete`, `listModels`). `anthropic.ts` speaks the Messages API (`x-api-key`, `anthropic-version`); `openaiCompat.ts` speaks `/chat/completions` and covers OpenAI, OpenRouter, Ollama, LM Studio and any custom base URL, retrying once with `max_completion_tokens` for newer OpenAI models. No vendor SDKs: each call is one `fetch`. `registry.ts#createAiProvider` is the only switch on `kind`; `AI_PRESETS` (Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, OpenRouter, Custom) carry base URL, default model, whether a key is needed, and the LiteLLM provider name used for pricing. HTTP and network failures are normalized into readable messages so raw provider JSON never reaches the UI. `fetch` is injectable so the adapters are unit-tested against a mock.
responsibilities: Send one completion request and return text plus exact input and output token counts and the server-reported model.
List the models an endpoint serves, with per-million prices where the endpoint publishes them (OpenRouter).
Turn 401/403/404/429/5xx and network errors into one readable sentence.
Hold the provider presets as data, including which LiteLLM provider prices each one.
Tell local endpoints (localhost, 127.0.0.1, ::1) apart for the consent gate.

dependsOn.why: Each adapter is a single HTTPS request to the provider's endpoint.

refs.note: Why two adapters and no SDKs.

components.name: AI usage and prices
components.summary: The local usage ledger, the fetched price table, the LiteLLM price list mirror and the 30-day trend.
components.detail: `usageStore.ts` appends one `UsageEntry` per call (time, provider, server-reported model, verb, exact tokens) to globalState, capped at 5,000 entries with the drop counted; per provider/model/verb running totals survive the cap so all-time stays exact. Cost is never stored: `estimateCost` multiplies tokens by the price `findPrice` returns at render time (exact provider+model, else the longest same-provider substring). `priceTable.ts` holds read-only `PriceRow`s, each labelled `api` or `litellm` with a `fetchedAt` that turns *stale* after 30 days. `litellmTable.ts` parses the LiteLLM community JSON (~1.6 MB) into ~129 KB of `[id, provider, in, out]` tuples and looks prices up scoped to one LiteLLM provider. `usageTrend.ts` buckets the ledger into UTC days for the chart host-side, counting unpriced calls rather than guessing them.
responsibilities: Append each call with exact token counts; cap the ledger and count what was dropped.
Keep all-time totals exact past the cap.
Compute estimated cost at render time; no price means '—', never $0.
Store fetched price rows with their source and age; mark rows over 30 days old as stale.
Store and query the local LiteLLM price list mirror.
Bucket the last 30 days into a stacked trend, by provider or by model.
Purge the ledger, price table, LiteLLM mirror and legacy price key on Reset All Data.

dependsOn.why: The ledger, price table and LiteLLM mirror live in VS Code globalState.

components.name: AI settings and keys
components.summary: AI provider settings, consent and the per-connection opt-out in globalState; each provider's API key in the OS keychain.
components.detail: `AiStore` keeps `AiSettings` (active provider, kind, base URL, model, per-provider form memory, the LiteLLM mapping for custom endpoints, `consentGiven`, `disabledConnections`) under `openDbClient.ai` in globalState, and each provider's API key in SecretStorage under `openDbClient.aiKey.<providerId>` — the same config/secret split as `ConnectionStore`. A blank key field on save means keep the stored key. `isConfigured` needs base URL and model, plus a key unless the preset (or a localhost URL) needs none. `deleteAll` purges settings and every known provider's key for Reset All Data. The module imports `vscode` as a type only, which lets `test/aiSettings.test.js` load it outside the extension host.
responsibilities: Persist provider settings and per-provider form memory.
Store, replace and delete one API key per provider in SecretStorage.
Answer whether AI is configured and whether it is enabled for a connection.
Hold the revocable consent flag and the list of connections AI is switched off for.
Purge everything on Reset All Data.

dependsOn.why: API keys go to the OS keychain, never to globalState.
Settings live in VS Code globalState.
Uses the preset list to know whether a provider needs a key.

components.name: AI providers and price list
components.summary: Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, a local Ollama or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint the user names, plus the LiteLLM price list on GitHub.
components.detail: The only internet-facing calls the extension makes from the host. Completion requests go straight from the user's machine to the provider they configured, with their own key — no proxy of ours in between. Model lists come from the same endpoint (`/v1/models` or `/models`); OpenRouter-style lists carry per-token prices, OpenAI and Anthropic publish none. The LiteLLM community price list (`raw.githubusercontent.com/BerriAI/litellm/main/model_prices_and_context_window.json`) is the labelled third-party fallback for providers whose APIs publish no prices. No provider billing or balance API is ever called; those need admin keys the extension deliberately never asks for.
responsibilities: Answer completion requests and report exact token usage in each response.
List the models an endpoint serves, with prices where the endpoint publishes them.
Publish the LiteLLM community price list the mirror is built from.

components.name: Settings & Guides
components.summary: The Settings & Guides webview: AI provider setup, consent, per-connection opt-out, usage, prices, and the data guides.
components.detail: A guides-style webview (`openDbClient.settings`) with a strict CSP (nonce'd inline script, no external fetch). Guides are entries in `GUIDES`; the AI Assistant guide holds the provider form (preset, base URL, model with a live ↻ model list, masked key, *Save* and *⚡ Test*), consent status with *Revoke*, the per-connection checkboxes, period and all-time usage tables, the 30-day trend chart, the read-only price table (*Load models* / *Add*, *＋ Price used models*, *↻ Refresh prices*) and the LiteLLM price list with *↻ Update price list*. *AI & your data* states what is and is not sent. *Uninstalling & your data* measures every stored key live (`storageUsage.ts`), counting secrets without reading them, and hosts the *Reset all data* button. Every AI message goes through `handleAiMessage`, which saves the form first (Test and model fetch use what is on screen) and calls `notifyAiSettingsChanged()` on save, opt-out and revoke.
responsibilities: Save the provider form: settings to globalState, a typed key to SecretStorage.
Run the Test round-trip and fetch the live model list.
Show and revoke consent; tick or untick AI per connection, reaching panels already open.
Show usage tables, the trend chart, the price table and the LiteLLM mirror with their status.
Explain what AI sees and where each thing is stored.
Measure stored data and trigger Reset All Data.

dependsOn.why: Test, model lists and every price-table action run through the AI service.
Reads and writes AI settings and keys.
Usage tables, trend and price rows are computed from the ledger and price table.
Lists connections for the opt-out checkboxes and counts their secrets.
The Reset all data button hands off to the reset command, which owns the confirm modal.
A VS Code webview panel; storage is measured from globalState and the storage folder.

components.name: Build and dev tooling
components.summary: esbuild bundles the extension into one file with the SQLite WASM beside it; typecheck, Biome lint and format; F5 debug.
components.detail: `esbuild.js` bundles `src/extension.ts` into `dist/extension.js` (CommonJS, node18), keeping `vscode` and the optional native accelerators (`pg-native`, `cpu-features`, any `.node`) external so the drivers fall back to pure JS, and copies `sql-wasm.wasm` into `dist/`. `--production` minifies; `--watch` rebuilds on save. `vscode:prepublish` runs typecheck plus the production bundle, so every `vsce package`/`publish` ships a fresh build. `.vscodeignore` keeps `src/`, `out/`, `node_modules/`, docs and scripts out of the `.vsix`. F5 (*Run Extension*) runs `npm: bundle` first via `.vscode/tasks.json`. Biome provides `lint`, `format` and `check`; lint-staged runs `biome check --write` on staged files.
responsibilities: Produce the shipped single-file bundle plus the SQLite WASM.
Typecheck without emitting.
Lint and format src and test with Biome.
Launch the Extension Development Host after a bundle.

components.name: Unit tests
components.summary: Plain node:test files over the tsc-compiled output; pure logic only, no VS Code API; run before every version bump.
components.detail: `npm test` compiles `src/` to `out/` with `tsc`, then runs `node --test test/*.test.js`. Tests are plain `.js` using `node:test`/`node:assert` and `require('../out/...')`, so anything under test must be exported from its `.ts` and must not need the VS Code runtime (hence `aiStore.ts` importing `vscode` as a type only). 26 files cover drivers' pure helpers, SQL completion and dialect, portability, the grid views, and the AI layer: `aiContext`, `aiProviders` (adapters against a mock `fetch`), `aiSettings`, `aiUsage`, `priceTable`, `litellmTable`, `usageTrend`, `storageUsage`. `preversion` runs the suite, so a failing test blocks `npm run release:*`. There is no CI pipeline in the repo; the manual QA checklists live in `docs/TESTING.md` and task.md QA gates.
responsibilities: Compile src to out and run every test file.
Exercise adapters with an injected fetch, never the network.
Block a release when anything fails.

dependsOn.why: Adapter parsing, usage extraction and error normalization are tested against a mock fetch.
Every schema-context export is unit-tested.
Ledger arithmetic, price lookup, LiteLLM parsing and trend bucketing are tested.

components.name: Versioning and publishing
components.summary: npm run release:* bumps, stamps the changelog, tags and packages locally; the publish scripts ship one .vsix to the Marketplace and Open VSX.
components.detail: `release:patch|minor|major` = `npm version` (preversion runs `npm test`; the `version` hook runs `scripts/stamp-changelog.mjs`, which turns `## [Unreleased]` into a dated `## [x.y.z]` section and stages it; npm commits and tags `vX.Y.Z`) then `npm run package`. Nothing is pushed. `publish:marketplace` (`scripts/publish.mjs`) calls `assertReleasedState` in `release-checks.mjs` (clean tree, stamped section for this version, tag warning), packages once, `vsce publish --packagePath`, optionally `ovsx publish` of the same file with `--ovsx` (checking `OVSX_PAT` up front), then pushes the commit and tags and cuts the GitHub release (`github-release.mjs`, non-fatal, notes from the changelog section). `publish:ovsx` publishes to Open VSX alone and refuses a version already live there. `marketplace:verify` compares live versions with local via the public gallery API and, with `--ovsx`, distinguishes an inactive upload under an unverified namespace from an unpublished one.
responsibilities: Keep package.json version and CHANGELOG sections in lock-step.
Refuse to publish from a dirty tree or an unstamped version.
Package once and send the same .vsix to both registries.
Push the release commit and tags only after a successful publish.
Create the GitHub release from the changelog section.
Report what is live on the Marketplace and Open VSX.

dependsOn.why: preversion runs the full suite before any bump.
Packaging runs vscode:prepublish: typecheck plus the production bundle.

components.name: Pre-commit secret scan
components.summary: Every commit runs Biome on staged files, then gitleaks over all history and over the staged change; no gitleaks means no commit.
components.detail: Husky (`prepare: husky`) installs `.husky/pre-commit`, which runs `npx lint-staged` (Biome `check --write` on staged `ts/js/mjs/json/jsonc`) and `sh scripts/gitleaks-scan.sh`. The script refuses the commit if gitleaks is not installed, then runs two passes with `--redact`: `gitleaks detect --log-opts=--all` over the committed history of every branch, and `gitleaks git --pre-commit --staged` over the change being committed, which a history scan cannot see. Also available as `npm run scan:secrets`.
responsibilities: Fix formatting and safe lint issues on staged files.
Scan full history and the staged change for secrets, printing findings redacted.
Refuse to commit unscanned when gitleaks is missing.

dependsOn.why: lint-staged applies the repo's Biome configuration.

journeys.title: A user adds a connection with the form and tests it
journeys.trigger: Clicks *Add Connection* (+) at the top of the Connections view
journeys.summary: A form opens, the user picks the engine and fills in the details, and can try the connection before saving it. Saving keeps the details in the extension's storage and the passwords in the system keychain.
rules: There is no limit on how many connections can be saved.
Passwords, SSH secrets and AWS secret keys go to the system keychain, never into the saved connection details.
*Test Connection* never saves anything; the trial connection is closed straight after.
When editing, a blank password box means keep the stored password.
Editing a connection keeps its place in the list; only new connections are added at the bottom.
Notes are optional, capped at 2,000 characters, stored unencrypted and included in exports, and the form says so.

steps.title: The form opens
steps.detail: A *New Connection* tab opens beside the editor. *Edit Connection* opens the same form filled in.
steps.tech: openDbClient.addConnection (view/title navigation@1) and openDbClient.editConnection call ConnectionFormPanel.open(); a WebviewPanel with a nonce'd CSP.

steps.title: The user picks an engine and fills in the fields
steps.detail: The fields change with the engine: host and port for servers, a file for SQLite, region and credentials for Athena. Missing required fields are flagged before anything is sent.
steps.tech: Engine chips toggle #netFields / #fileFields / #athenaFields and set the default port from DEFAULT_PORTS; validate() requires name, then file path (SQLite), region and access key (Athena keys mode) or host.

steps.title: *Test Connection* tries a real connection
steps.detail: It connects exactly as a saved connection would, including through the SSH tunnel, then closes it. When editing, stored passwords fill in for blank boxes.
steps.tech: 'test' message → test(): toConfig(), openTunnelForConfig() if sshEnabled && type !== sqlite, createDriver(effective).connect({ password, awsSecretAccessKey, awsSessionToken }); finally driver.dispose() and tunnel.close().

steps.title: The result shows beside the button
steps.detail: A green tick or the server's error message, with how long it took. A long error shows in full on hover.
steps.tech: Host posts { type: 'testResult', ok, message, ms }; banner() renders it in the fixed footer with 'Cost: Nms' and sets title to the full text.

steps.title: *Save* stores the details and the secrets separately
steps.detail: Any open copy of this connection is closed first so the next use picks up the new settings. Details go to the extension's storage, each secret to the keychain.
steps.tech: 'save' → save(): toConfig() (notes trimmed to NOTES_MAX_CHARS), manager.disconnect(id), store.save(config, secrets): globalState 'openDbClient.connections' replaced in place and stamped schemaVersion; storeSecret() writes only non-empty values to SecretStorage.

steps.title: *Save & Connect* also opens it
steps.detail: If the save worked but the connect did not, the user is told both.
steps.tech: thenConnect → manager.getDriver(id); on error 'Saved, but connect failed: …'.

steps.title: The connection appears in the tree
steps.detail: With its engine icon and, if notes were written, the notes on hover.
steps.tech: refresh callback → tree.refresh(); root nodes are store.all() in saved order, contextValue connection / connectionActive.

checks.question: Does pressing Test Connection save the connection?
checks.answer: No. It opens a trial connection, reports the result and how long it took, and closes it again. Only Save or Save & Connect store anything.

checks.question: Where does the password typed into the form end up?
checks.answer: In the system keychain, filed under that connection. The saved connection details do not contain it.

journeys.title: A user connects to a database behind an SSH jump host
journeys.actor: Developer whose database is only reachable through a bastion
journeys.trigger: Turns on *Use SSH Tunnel* in the form, then connects
journeys.summary: Before the database connection is made, the extension signs in to the SSH server and forwards a port on this machine to the database. The database connection then goes to that local port.
rules: Offered for PostgreSQL, MySQL and Redis; not for SQLite (a local file) or Athena (no host to tunnel to).
*Auto* tries the SSH agent, then a key (your chosen file, or your default SSH key), then the password.
An encrypted default key with no passphrase given is skipped instead of failing the whole sign-in.
The SSH handshake waits 5 seconds by default, and opening the tunnel gives up after 15 seconds.
SSH passwords and key passphrases are kept in the system keychain like database passwords.
Closing the connection closes its tunnel.

steps.title: The user fills in the SSH section
steps.detail: SSH host, port (22 by default), user, sign-in method and a connect timeout. The section only exists for engines that have a host.
steps.tech: #sshBox lives inside #netFields, hidden for sqlite and athena; sshAuth defaults to 'auto', sshConnectTimeout to 5000 ms.

steps.title: SSH secrets go to the keychain
steps.detail: Saved under the connection, separately from the database password.
steps.tech: store.save(): openDbClient.sshPassword.<id> and openDbClient.sshPassphrase.<id> in SecretStorage.

steps.title: On connect, the tunnel is opened first
steps.detail: The SSH secrets are read from the keychain and the tunnel must be up within 15 seconds.
steps.tech: getDriver(): if config.sshEnabled && type !== 'sqlite' → withTimeout(openTunnelForConfig(config, { sshPassword, sshPassphrase }), TUNNEL_OPEN_TIMEOUT_MS = 15 000, 'SSH tunnel').

steps.title: The tunnel works out where the database really is
steps.detail: From the host and port fields, or by reading them out of the connection string.
steps.tech: openTunnelForConfig(): csTarget(connectionString, DEFAULT_PORTS[type]) or config.host/port; an unparseable string fails with 'Invalid connection string — cannot parse host for SSH tunnel'.

steps.title: It signs in to the SSH server
steps.detail: Using the chosen method; *Auto* tries agent, key and password in turn. If the server does not answer in time, the error names SSH.
steps.tech: buildConnectConfig(): agent = SSH_AUTH_SOCK; resolvePrivateKey(): explicit path (~ expanded) or first of id_ed25519, id_rsa, id_ecdsa that ssh2.utils.parseKey accepts; readyTimeout = sshConnectTimeout ?? 5000; errors prefixed 'SSH: '.

steps.title: A local port is forwarded to the database
steps.detail: A free port on this machine is picked, and the connection details are rewritten to point at it.
steps.tech: net.createServer().listen(0, '127.0.0.1'); each socket → client.forwardOut(targetHost, targetPort); effectiveConfig = host/port 127.0.0.1:<port>, or csRewriteHostPort() for strings (keeps user, password, database, query).

steps.title: The database connects through the local port
steps.detail: The engine's own connection is made as if the database were on this machine.
steps.tech: createDriver(effectiveConfig).connect(secrets); tunnel kept in the tunnels map by id.

steps.title: Closing the connection closes the tunnel
steps.detail: The database connection is closed first, then the SSH connection.
steps.tech: disconnect(id): driver.dispose(), then tunnel.close() (server.close(), client.end()).

checks.question: With Auto and no key file chosen, will the extension use my usual SSH key?
checks.answer: Yes. It tries the SSH agent, then the first default key in your SSH folder that it can open, then the password.

checks.question: How long does a dead SSH host take to fail?
checks.answer: The SSH handshake waits 5 seconds by default (adjustable in the form), and opening the tunnel is cut off at 15 seconds either way.

journeys.title: A connection is opened, fails or hangs, and is closed
journeys.trigger: Expands a connection in the tree, or chooses *Connect*
journeys.summary: Connections open only when first needed and are reused after that. A failure shows the server's message in the tree; a hang is cut off, and *Stop All Connections* can always clear a stuck one without restarting VS Code.
rules: A connection opens only when you expand it, choose *Connect*, or run something against it.
A failed connection shows a warning row with the real error, and anything half-built is closed.
Time limits: SSH tunnel 15 seconds; PostgreSQL, MySQL and Redis connect 10 seconds; loading tree items 20 seconds.
A time limit only stops waiting; the attempt is cleaned up when it fails or when *Stop All* runs.
*Stop All Connections* closes every connection, including ones still trying to connect.
Closing VS Code closes every connection the same way.

steps.title: Expanding a connection opens it
steps.detail: The first expand connects; the icon switches to connected once it is up.
steps.tech: getChildren(element) → manager.getDriver(connectionId); if it was not connected before, fire a refresh so the root node becomes connectionActive.

steps.title: An open connection is reused
steps.detail: Later expands and queries use the same connection.
steps.tech: getDriver(): return live.get(id) when present.

steps.title: A new attempt is recorded before it starts
steps.detail: So that it can still be stopped if it never finishes.
steps.tech: pending.set(id, {}) before tunnel and driver are built; driver/tunnel attached as they appear; pending.delete(id) in finally.

steps.title: Stored secrets are handed to the engine
steps.detail: The extension reads them from the keychain; the engine code never reads the keychain itself.
steps.tech: driver.connect({ password: store.getPassword(id), awsSecretAccessKey, awsSessionToken }); ConnectSecrets in Driver.ts.

steps.title: The engine gives up after 10 seconds
steps.detail: PostgreSQL, MySQL and Redis each ask for a 10-second connect limit.
steps.tech: pg connectionTimeoutMillis 10 000; mysql2 connectTimeout 10 000; ioredis connectTimeout 10 000.

steps.title: A failure is cleaned up and shown
steps.detail: Whatever was half-built is closed, the error goes to the log, and the tree shows a warning row with the message. *Connect* also shows it as an error pop-up.
steps.tech: catch: logError('connect:<type>:<name>'), pend.driver.dispose(), tunnel.close(), rethrow; tree catch renders a DbNode labelled '⚠ <message>' with contextValue 'error'; openDbClient.connect shows 'Connect failed: …'.

steps.title: Loading a level of the tree is capped at 20 seconds
steps.detail: A slow metadata read turns into an error row instead of a spinner that never ends.
steps.tech: withTimeout(driver.children(...), CHILDREN_TIMEOUT_MS = 20 000, 'Loading') → 'Loading timed out after 20s'.

steps.title: *Close Connection* closes one
steps.detail: The icon on a connected row closes that connection and its tunnel, and collapses it.
steps.tech: openDbClient.disconnect (inline@2, viewItem == connectionActive) → manager.disconnect(id) + tree.markDisconnected(id) (bumps the node generation).

steps.title: *Stop All Connections* clears everything
steps.detail: Every open connection, every attempt still in progress and every tunnel is closed, and the tree collapses. One failure does not stop the rest.
steps.tech: openDbClient.stopAll → manager.disposeAll(): allSettled dispose over live + pending drivers, try/catch close over every tunnel; tree.markAllDisconnected() bumps every generation and clears key filters.

steps.title: Closing VS Code does the same
steps.detail: The extension's clean-up runs the same full teardown.
steps.tech: ctx.subscriptions.push({ dispose: () => manager.disposeAll() }).

checks.question: A connection is stuck on a spinner. Do I need to restart VS Code?
checks.answer: No. Stop All Connections closes it even while it is still trying to connect.

checks.question: What does the user see when the password is wrong?
checks.answer: A warning row in the tree with the server's own error message (and an error pop-up if they chose Connect).

journeys.title: A user exports their connections to a file
journeys.actor: Developer moving machines, sharing a starting set, or backing up
journeys.trigger: Chooses *Export Connections…* from the Connections view's … menu
journeys.summary: One picker offers three kinds of file, safest first: without passwords, with passwords encrypted by a passphrase, or with passwords in plain text behind a confirmation. The file never carries the local connection ids.
rules: The default *Without passwords* file holds no stored passwords, and a password written inside a connection string is stripped; usernames are kept.
Notes travel in every kind of export, including *Without passwords*, and the picker says so.
An encrypted file needs the passphrase to open; there is no recovery if it is lost.
Plain text needs an explicit confirmation that states how many passwords will be exposed, and offers the encrypted file instead.
If no connection has a password, plain text falls back to the normal export and says why.
Files that carry passwords are made readable only by their owner where the disk allows it.

steps.title: The picker lists three choices, safest first
steps.detail: Each line says what the file will contain, so the trade-off is visible before choosing.
steps.tech: openDbClient.exportConnections (view/title group 1_portability) → showQuickPick(EXPORT_MODES: redacted, encrypted, plaintext).

steps.title: Secrets are read only if the choice includes them
steps.detail: For the passwordless file the keychain is not touched at all.
steps.tech: includeSecrets = mode !== 'redacted'; per config getPassword / getSshPassword / getSshPassphrase / getAwsSecret / getAwsSessionToken.

steps.title: Plain text asks for confirmation with real counts
steps.detail: The warning counts database passwords, SSH secrets and passwords inside connection strings, and offers the encrypted file as a button.
steps.tech: countSecrets() + countEmbeddedCredentials(); total 0 → doExport('redacted'); modal with 'Export in plain text' / 'Use the encrypted export instead'.

steps.title: Encrypted asks for a passphrase twice
steps.detail: At least 8 characters, typed twice so a typo is caught now rather than on the other machine.
steps.tech: promptNewPassphrase(): two password InputBoxes, min length 8, must match.

steps.title: The file is built without local ids
steps.detail: Without passwords: stored secrets left out and any password removed from connection strings, with those entries flagged. Otherwise the secrets are added.
steps.tech: buildExport(): drops id and schemaVersion; redactConnectionString() (URL parse, textual fallback, never fails open) sets redactedCredentials; SECRET_FIELDS copied only when includeSecrets; plaintext stamps a warning field.

steps.title: The encrypted file is sealed with the passphrase
steps.detail: A tampered file or wrong passphrase cannot be opened later.
steps.tech: encryptBundle(): scrypt(N=16384, r=8, p=1, random 16-byte salt) → AES-256-GCM with random 12-byte IV; kind 'open-db-client/connections-encrypted'.

steps.title: The file is written
steps.detail: The file name says what it is (encrypted, or PLAINTEXT). Files with passwords are restricted to the owner.
steps.tech: showSaveDialog default 'open-db-client-connections.{json|encrypted.json|PLAINTEXT.json}'; writeFileSync with mode 0o600 then best-effort chmodSync when includeSecrets.

steps.title: The summary says what happened
steps.detail: It names connections whose connection-string password was stripped, or warns to delete a plain-text file.
steps.tech: Info / warning toast per mode; redactedNames listed for the redacted export.

checks.question: If a connection was saved from a connection string with a password in it, does the passwordless export contain that password?
checks.answer: No. The password is stripped from the string, the entry is flagged, and the summary names that connection. The username stays.

checks.question: Are connection notes left out of the passwordless export?
checks.answer: No. Notes go into every export, and the picker says so.

journeys.title: A user imports connections from a file
journeys.actor: Developer setting up a second machine or receiving a team's set
journeys.trigger: Chooses *Import Connections…* from the Connections view's … menu
journeys.summary: The file is read as untrusted input, checked, and only ever added to the existing list. Connections already saved are skipped, and the user sees the counts before anything is written.
rules: Import only adds; existing connections are never changed, reordered or removed.
A connection pointing at a server you already have is skipped, even under a different name.
A different server with a name you already use is added as "(imported)".
Unknown fields are dropped, bad entries are skipped and counted, and the reasons go to the Output panel.
A file from a newer version of the extension is refused with a request to update.
A wrong passphrase and a tampered file give the same error.

steps.title: The user picks a file
steps.detail: Any of the three export kinds; the user does not have to say which.
steps.tech: openDbClient.importConnections → showOpenDialog({ filters: JSON }) → readFileSync.

steps.title: An encrypted file asks for its passphrase
steps.detail: Recognised by its contents, not its name. Wrong passphrase or a modified file stops here with a clear message.
steps.tech: isEncryptedBundle(text) → password InputBox → decryptBundle(): kind/version/cipher/kdf checks, GCM auth tag; 'Wrong passphrase, or the file has been modified.'

steps.title: The file is checked as untrusted
steps.detail: Only known fields of the right kind are kept, because some are file paths the extension will later read or addresses it will dial.
steps.tech: parseImport(): kind 'open-db-client/connections' and version ≤ EXPORT_VERSION; sanitize() keeps STRING_FIELDS / NUMBER_FIELDS / BOOL_FIELDS / SECRET_FIELDS by type, validates sshAuth and awsAuthMode, caps notes at NOTES_MAX_CHARS; one warning per skipped entry.

steps.title: Duplicates are skipped and clashes renamed
steps.detail: The same server saved under another name, or as a connection string instead of fields, still counts as the same.
steps.tech: mergeConnections(): identityKey() = type|host|port|database|username via resolveTarget() (sqlite: filePath; redis: redisDb); uniqueName() adds ' (imported)' / ' (imported N)'; mkId() gives every entry a fresh id.

steps.title: The user confirms with the counts in front of them
steps.detail: How many will be added and how many skipped; nothing is written before this.
steps.tech: Modal 'Import N connection(s)? M already saved and will be skipped. Your existing connections are not changed.'

steps.title: New connections are saved
steps.detail: Each is added at the end of the list; database passwords and SSH secrets from the file go into the system keychain under the new connection.
steps.tech: for added: store.save(config, secrets.get(config.id)); secrets map keyed by the new id.

steps.title: The summary reports what happened
steps.detail: Added and skipped counts, a note if the file had no passwords, and how many entries were dropped.
steps.tech: Info toast; warnTail() points at View → Output → 'Open DB Client' where each warning was logged.

checks.question: What happens if I import the same file twice?
checks.answer: The second time nothing is added: every connection is recognised as already saved and skipped, and the summary says so.

checks.question: Can an import overwrite one of my existing connections?
checks.answer: No. Import only adds new entries at the end; existing ones are never modified, reordered or removed.

journeys.title: A user sets up a connection from a pasted connection string
journeys.actor: Developer who has a database URL from a provider or a teammate
journeys.trigger: Turns on *Use Connection String* in the form and pastes a URL
journeys.summary: The user can either connect with the string as given, or press *Use* to copy its parts into the separate fields. With an SSH tunnel on, the host and port are read from the string and pointed at the tunnel.
rules: The *Use* button copies host, port, user, password and database into the separate fields; it reports when the string cannot be read.
For the password to be kept in the system keychain, save it in the separate password field; the in-app guide says so.
With the toggle on, the engine connects with the string as written.
With SSH on, only the host and port in the string are changed; user, database and options are kept.
Exports without passwords strip any password from the string and keep the rest.

steps.title: The user turns on the toggle and pastes the string
steps.detail: The box shows an example for the chosen engine.
steps.tech: #useCS toggles #csRow; CS_PLACEHOLDER per engine (postgresql://, mysql://, redis://).

steps.title: *Use* fills the separate fields from it
steps.detail: Host, port, user, password and database (or Redis database number) are copied across, with a banner saying it worked or could not parse the string.
steps.tech: csUse click → new URL(raw); hostname/port/username/password (decodeURIComponent)/pathname → fields; banner('Parsed connection string into fields' | 'Could not parse connection string').

steps.title: The in-app guide steers passwords to the separate fields
steps.detail: It explains that the separate password field is the one kept in the keychain and suggests re-saving string-based connections that way.
steps.tech: Settings & Guides → 'Uninstalling & your data' caveat block.

steps.title: With the toggle on, the engine connects with the string
steps.detail: PostgreSQL, MySQL and Redis are given the string directly.
steps.tech: useConnectionString → mysql.createPool(connectionString), new Redis(connectionString, options); Postgres builds its pool from the string (and rewrites the database segment per pool).

steps.title: With SSH on, the string is pointed at the tunnel
steps.detail: The host and port are read out of it for the tunnel, then replaced with the local forwarded port.
steps.tech: csTarget() for the target; csRewriteHostPort(cs, '127.0.0.1', localPort) keeps user/pass/db/query (tested in connString.test.js).

steps.title: Exports strip the password from the string
steps.detail: In the passwordless export only the password is removed; the entry is flagged so the importer knows to add it.
steps.tech: redactConnectionString(): URL parse and clear password, or textual 'scheme://user:pass@' fallback; redactedCredentials: true.

checks.question: After pressing Use, which fields are filled in?
checks.answer: Host, port, user, password and database (or the Redis database number), as far as the string contains them.

checks.question: With an SSH tunnel, what parts of the string change?
checks.answer: Only the host and port, which are pointed at the local end of the tunnel. User, database and options stay as written.

journeys.title: A user removes everything the extension has stored
journeys.actor: Developer about to uninstall, or clearing a machine
journeys.trigger: Presses *Reset all data* in Settings & Guides, or runs *Reset All Data* from the command palette
journeys.summary: Uninstalling the extension leaves saved connections, keychain passwords and query files behind, so Reset All Data is the one-click way to remove them. It keeps going if a single step fails and reports what may remain.
rules: Uninstalling does not remove saved connections, stored passwords or query files; VS Code keeps them.
Reset asks once, in a modal, and cannot be undone.
To keep a backup, export with passwords encrypted first; the guide says so.
If some keychain entries cannot be deleted, the connections are still cleared and the user is told how many secrets may remain.
AI provider keys, AI settings and the AI usage record are removed too.

steps.title: The user starts Reset All Data
steps.detail: From the button at the bottom of Settings & Guides, or the command palette.
steps.tech: settingsPanel posts 'resetAllData' → executeCommand('openDbClient.resetAllData').

steps.title: One modal confirmation
steps.detail: It lists what will go and says it cannot be undone.
steps.tech: showWarningMessage(..., { modal: true }, 'Remove Everything').

steps.title: Every connection is closed
steps.detail: Including tunnels and attempts still in progress.
steps.tech: manager.disposeAll().

steps.title: Every connection's secrets and the list are deleted
steps.detail: All five kinds of secret per connection are removed from the keychain; the list is cleared even if some deletes fail.
steps.tech: store.deleteAll(): Promise.allSettled over password / sshPassword / sshPassphrase / awsSecret / awsSessionToken per id, then globalState 'openDbClient.connections' = []; returns secretsFailed.

steps.title: Saved query files are deleted
steps.detail: The whole folder of saved .sql files goes.
steps.tech: queries.deleteAll() under globalStorageUri.

steps.title: AI keys, settings and usage are deleted
steps.detail: For every built-in provider and the custom one in use.
steps.tech: AiStore.deleteAll([...AI_PRESETS ids, active providerId]); UsageStore.deleteAll().

steps.title: The result is reported honestly
steps.detail: Either all removed, or a warning with how many secrets may still be in the keychain, or an error saying some data may remain. The tree is refreshed in every case.
steps.tech: secretsFailed > 0 → warning; catch → error; finally tree.refresh().

steps.title: Without a reset, uninstall leaves it all behind
steps.detail: VS Code keeps the extension's storage, keychain entries and storage folder after uninstall; the in-app guide says so.
steps.tech: globalState, SecretStorage and globalStorageUri are not cleared by VS Code on uninstall.

checks.question: If I uninstall the extension, are my saved passwords removed?
checks.answer: No. VS Code keeps them. Run Reset All Data first if you want nothing left behind.

checks.question: What happens if one keychain entry refuses to delete?
checks.answer: The reset carries on, the saved connections are still cleared, and a warning says how many secrets may still be in the keychain.

journeys.title: A user expands a connection down to its tables
journeys.trigger: Clicks the arrow next to a saved connection in the Open DB Client sidebar
journeys.summary: Expanding a connection connects to it if needed and shows everything on the server, not just one database: databases, then schemas, then tables and views, then their columns, indexes, foreign keys and triggers.
rules: Expanding a connection connects it on the spot, using the saved password from the system keychain.
PostgreSQL shows every database on the server, including ones this login cannot enter, which are marked as such.
SQLite has no database level: the file is the database, so its tables appear straight away.
An expansion that takes longer than 20 seconds stops and shows the error in the tree instead of spinning forever.
Every database and schema also gets a Query folder for saved query files.

steps.title: The user expands a connection
steps.detail: The tree asks for a connected driver, connecting first if this is the first use.
steps.tech: getChildren → manager.getDriver(id) → driver.children([], filter) wrapped in withTimeout(CHILDREN_TIMEOUT_MS = 20 s).

steps.title: The right engine is chosen and connected
steps.detail: The saved connection's type picks the engine, and secrets are handed to it from secure storage.
steps.tech: createDriver(config) by config.type; driver.connect({password, awsSecretAccessKey, awsSessionToken}). SSH tunnel opened first when enabled (not SQLite).

steps.title: The server's databases are listed
steps.detail: PostgreSQL lists every database plus a Security folder of users and roles; MySQL lists its databases; Redis lists its numbered databases with key counts; Athena lists data catalogs.
steps.tech: pg_database WHERE datistemplate = false (datallowconn=false → 'no connect'); information_schema.schemata minus system schemas; CONFIG GET databases + INFO keyspace; ListDataCatalogs.

steps.title: Each PostgreSQL database opens its own pool
steps.detail: Opening a database connects to it separately, so tables in any database on the server can be browsed and edited.
steps.tech: pools: Map<db, Pool> (max 4 each), created lazily by poolFor(key); connection-string mode rewrites the URL path per database.

steps.title: Schemas, then tables and views, appear
steps.detail: Each level lists its children in name order; views get their own icon.
steps.tech: information_schema.schemata / information_schema.tables (table_type VIEW → kind 'view').

steps.title: A table opens into four folders
steps.detail: Columns, Indexes, Foreign Keys and Triggers, with column types and key markers shown beside each column.
steps.tech: tableFolders(path) appends sentinels @columns/@indexes/@fk/@triggers; MySQL and SQLite reuse it.

steps.title: The tree adds icons, Query folders and click behaviour
steps.detail: Database and schema rows get a Query folder; table rows preview on click everywhere except Athena.
steps.tech: toNode(): kind → contextValue (database-redis, table-noclick); queryRootNode() unshifted for database/schema.

steps.title: A failure shows inline
steps.detail: If the server refuses or times out, the row shows the error message instead of children.
steps.tech: catch → DbNode with contextValue 'error' and ThemeIcon('error').

checks.question: Why might a PostgreSQL database be listed even though you cannot open it?
checks.answer: The tree lists every database on the server, including ones your login cannot enter; those are marked no connect and show the refusal when expanded.

checks.question: What happens if expanding a node hangs?
checks.answer: After 20 seconds it stops and shows the error as a row in the tree.

journeys.title: A user previews a table's rows
journeys.trigger: Clicks a table or view in the tree (or chooses Preview Rows)
journeys.summary: Clicking a table opens a grid of its first 100 rows, with paging, sort and filters done by the database, the equivalent SQL shown in the editor, and in-place editing when the table has a primary key.
rules: A preview reads 100 rows at a time and pages forward and back; the total row count drives the pager.
Rows can be edited in place only when the table has a primary key; otherwise the grid is read-only.
The SQL shown in the editor is the readable equivalent of the preview and can be edited and run.
On Athena a click never starts a preview, because every preview is a billed query; Preview Rows is an explicit action there and does not page.
Limits are always stated in the grid, never applied silently.

steps.title: The user clicks a table
steps.detail: On PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and Redis keys a click previews; on Athena it only expands and a Preview Rows button appears instead.
steps.tech: node.command = openDbClient.previewTable unless isAthena; Athena tables carry contextValue '*-noclick', which shows Preview Rows inline.

steps.title: A query panel opens for that table
steps.detail: The command opens a panel bound to the table's path.
steps.tech: QueryPanel.create(ctx, manager, store, id, { previewPath: node.nodePath }); viewKey is the same action with a Redis-friendly title.

steps.title: The panel asks for the first page
steps.detail: It requests 100 rows with the current sort and column filters.
steps.tech: runPreview → driver.previewTable(path, { offset, limit: PAGE_SIZE (100), filter, sort, columnFilters }).

steps.title: The driver reads the page safely
steps.detail: Table and column names are quoted and filter values are sent as parameters, then the column details, foreign keys and total count are read.
steps.tech: SELECT * FROM qi(schema).qi(table) WHERE … LIMIT n OFFSET m with $1.. params; tableColumns → columnsMeta + editable {table, pkColumns}; page.total from countRows().

steps.title: The grid shows rows, editing and the matching SQL
steps.detail: Primary-key columns make cells editable; the editor shows the equivalent SELECT.
steps.tech: QueryResult.sql from displaySql(qualified, opts, 'ILIKE'|'LIKE'); values inlined for display only.

steps.title: On Athena, one bounded statement is the whole preview
steps.detail: It runs a single capped SELECT, shows exactly that statement, reports no total beyond the rows in hand, and warns that going further is a new billed query.
steps.tech: limit = min(opts.limit ?? 500, 500) → with the panel's 100 this is 100; page.total = rows.length so the pager stops; no countRows.

steps.title: A Redis key preview states its own cap
steps.detail: A list or sorted set shows its first 200 elements and says how many it holds in total.
steps.tech: LRANGE/ZRANGE 0..199 + LLEN/ZCARD → previewNotice(shown, total, unit).

checks.question: Why does clicking an Athena table not show its rows?
checks.answer: Every Athena preview is a billed query, so a stray click must not start one; previewing is the explicit Preview Rows action.

checks.question: When can you edit a previewed row?
checks.answer: Only when the table has a primary key.

journeys.title: A user views a table's DDL
journeys.trigger: Right-clicks a table or view and chooses View DDL / Structure
journeys.summary: The table's CREATE statement opens as a read-only-in-spirit SQL document. Some engines return the server's own text; others rebuild it from catalog details and say it is approximate.
rules: MySQL returns the server's own CREATE TABLE text, and SQLite returns the statement stored in the file.
PostgreSQL and Athena rebuild the statement from catalog details and label it approximate, because it is the table's shape rather than a statement that would recreate it exactly.
Athena's rebuilt DDL uses Athena's own DDL quoting, which differs from its query quoting.
Redis has no tables, so asking for DDL shows an error instead.

steps.title: The user picks View DDL / Structure
steps.detail: The menu item appears on tables and views.
steps.tech: openDbClient.showDDL when viewItem =~ /table|view/ → driver.getDDL(node.nodePath).

steps.title: MySQL hands back its own definition
steps.detail: The server's own statement is shown unchanged.
steps.tech: SHOW CREATE TABLE `db`.`table` → 'Create Table' or 'Create View'.

steps.title: SQLite returns the stored statement
steps.detail: SQLite keeps the original CREATE text in the file, so it is shown as written.
steps.tech: SELECT sql FROM sqlite_master WHERE name = ? (parameterized).

steps.title: PostgreSQL rebuilds an approximate one
steps.detail: Columns, types, not-null and the primary key are assembled and marked approximate.
steps.tech: From information_schema columns + pg_index primary key; header '-- Reconstructed from information_schema (approximate)'.

steps.title: Athena rebuilds one from table metadata
steps.detail: Columns, partition columns and storage location are included; the header says the storage format details are missing.
steps.tech: GetTableMetadata → CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE with qDdl() backticks and hiveStr() for LOCATION; no query is run.

steps.title: The text opens as a SQL document
steps.detail: It opens in an editor tab; any failure shows as an error message.
steps.tech: workspace.openTextDocument({ content: ddl, language: 'sql' }) → showTextDocument(preview: true); Redis getDDL throws 'DDL is not applicable to Redis'.

checks.question: Is the PostgreSQL DDL safe to run to recreate the table exactly?
checks.answer: No. It is rebuilt from catalog details and labelled approximate.

journeys.title: A user searches the tables in a schema
journeys.trigger: Clicks the search icon on a database or schema row and types
journeys.summary: A live search box narrows the table and view list as you type, and a pinned Filter row shows the term and how many match; clicking it clears the search.
rules: Search narrows table, view, schema and database names; the Query folder is always kept.
For SQL databases the matching happens in the tree itself, because table lists are small enough that it is instant.
The pinned Filter row shows the number of matches and clears the search when clicked.
Disconnecting everything drops all search terms.

steps.title: The user opens Search Tables
steps.detail: The search icon sits on database and schema rows (PostgreSQL schemas, MySQL databases).
steps.tech: openDbClient.searchTables when viewItem =~ /^(database|schema)$/ → liveFilterInput(debounceMs: 150).

steps.title: Typing updates the filter after a short pause
steps.detail: Each pause in typing saves the term for that row and redraws it.
steps.tech: createInputBox; onDidChangeValue → setTimeout(tree.setKeyFilter(node, value), 150 ms); Enter applies at once.

steps.title: The tree narrows the list
steps.detail: The driver lists everything as usual; the tree then keeps only names containing the term.
steps.tech: Case-insensitive includes() over STRUCTURAL context values; non-structural rows pass through. Athena also passes the term to Glue as ListTableMetadata Expression.

steps.title: A pinned Filter row shows the result
steps.detail: It reads the term and the match count; clicking it clears the search.
steps.tech: listFilterNode() with contextValue 'keyfilter' → openDbClient.clearKeyFilter(path minus @keyfilter).

checks.question: Does searching tables send a query to the database on each keystroke?
checks.answer: No for PostgreSQL and MySQL: the list is narrowed in the tree itself. Athena passes the term to its metadata lookup.

journeys.title: A user searches Redis keys
journeys.trigger: Clicks the search icon on a Redis db row and types part of a key name
journeys.summary: The key list re-filters as you type, using Redis's own incremental key walk with a match pattern, so a large database stays responsive and the list never silently stops at its 500-key cap.
rules: Plain text matches anywhere in the key; text with glob characters such as an asterisk is used as typed.
The search runs on the Redis server, not in the tree.
The list shows at most 500 keys; when there are more, it says so and points at the search.
Keys are sorted by name, and keys that expire show their remaining life.
Clicking the pinned Filter row clears the search.

steps.title: The user opens Search Keys on a db row
steps.detail: The search box explains that matching is server-side and that globs work.
steps.tech: openDbClient.searchKeys when viewItem == database-redis → liveFilterInput(debounceMs: 300).

steps.title: The term is passed down to the driver
steps.detail: After each pause in typing the tree redraws that db row with the term attached.
steps.tech: keyFilters Map keyed by connectionId:path; driver.children(path, filter).

steps.title: The term becomes a match pattern
steps.detail: Plain text is wrapped to match anywhere; glob text is kept.
steps.tech: scanPattern('order') → '*order*'; any of * ? [ ] → verbatim.

steps.title: Redis is walked in small batches
steps.detail: The driver asks for keys a batch at a time until it has 500 or runs out of round trips, and records whether it stopped early.
steps.tech: SELECT db; SCAN cursor MATCH p COUNT 500, up to 200 round trips filtered (20 unfiltered); truncated = more found or cursor ≠ 0.

steps.title: Keys are sorted and their expiry read in one go
steps.detail: Keys with an expiry show it beside the name.
steps.tech: keys.sort(); one pipelined PTTL per key; formatTtl(ms) when ms > 0.

steps.title: A pinned row states what you are seeing
steps.detail: With a search it shows the term and the match count, with a plus when capped; without one, a capped list shows Showing first 500 keys.
steps.tech: info node path [db, '@keyfilter'] (→ contextValue keyfilter, click clears) or [db, '@keytruncated'].

checks.question: What does typing user: search for?
checks.answer: Any key containing user: anywhere, because plain text is wrapped to match anywhere.

checks.question: What happens in a database with 10,000 keys and no search?
checks.answer: The first 500 are listed, and a row says Showing first 500 keys and suggests searching.

journeys.title: A user views a Redis key's value
journeys.trigger: Clicks a key in the tree, or right-clicks it and chooses View Value
journeys.summary: The key opens in the grid shaped by its type, so each element can be edited on its own, with the key's remaining time to live shown in the toolbar.
rules: A string shows one value; a list shows position and value; a hash shows field and value; a set shows members; a sorted set shows member and score.
Lists and sorted sets show their first 200 elements and say how many there are in total.
Editing a string keeps its expiry rather than making it permanent.
Deleting a row in the grid removes only that element, never the whole key.
Other key types are shown read-only.

steps.title: The user clicks a key
steps.detail: Keys preview on click like tables do.
steps.tech: kind 'key' → openDbClient.previewTable; menu item View Value = openDbClient.viewKey (same handler).

steps.title: The driver checks the key's type
steps.detail: It switches to the key's numbered database and asks what kind of value it holds.
steps.tech: SELECT db; TYPE key; readValue(type, key); sql = previewCommandFor(type, key).

steps.title: The value is shaped for the grid
steps.detail: Each type gets columns that let one element be addressed; long lists and sorted sets are cut at 200 with a notice.
steps.tech: LRANGE/LLEN, HGETALL, SMEMBERS, ZRANGE WITHSCORES/ZCARD, GET; PK_COLUMN gives the editable column per type.

steps.title: Its time to live is attached
steps.detail: The grid shows how long the key has left, or that it never expires.
steps.tech: result.ttl = PTTL key (-1 no expiry, -2 gone).

steps.title: Edits go back element by element
steps.detail: Changing a cell updates that one element; a string edit carries its expiry across.
steps.tech: updateCell: PTTL → SET → PEXPIRE for strings; LSET; HSET/rename; SADD+SREM; ZADD. deleteRow with a pk removes only the element.

checks.question: If you edit a string key that expires in 60 seconds, does it become permanent?
checks.answer: No. The remaining expiry is read first and put back after the edit.

journeys.title: A user sets or clears a key's expiry
journeys.trigger: Right-clicks a key and chooses Set TTL / Expiry…, or uses Set TTL… or Persist in the grid toolbar
journeys.summary: A native input box asks for seconds until the key expires; a blank or zero answer makes the key permanent.
rules: The answer must be a whole number of seconds; anything else is refused in the box.
Blank or zero removes the expiry, so the key stays forever.
If the key has disappeared in the meantime, the change is refused with a clear message.
Only engines that have expiry offer this; others say the connection does not support it.

steps.title: The user asks to set the expiry
steps.detail: From the tree's right-click menu or the grid toolbar.
steps.tech: openDbClient.setTtl (tree) or webview message 'setTtl' → QueryPanel.handleSetTtl('edit'|'persist').

steps.title: A native box asks for seconds
steps.detail: In the grid it is prefilled with the current remaining time.
steps.tech: window.showInputBox with validateInput: integer ≥ 0; prefill from lastResult.ttl / 1000.

steps.title: The engine is checked for expiry support
steps.detail: Engines without the concept never get a pretend version of it.
steps.tech: if (!driver.setTtl) → 'This connection does not support TTL.' (optional Driver member).

steps.title: Redis applies or removes the expiry
steps.detail: It first checks the key still exists, then sets the new life or makes the key permanent.
steps.tech: EXISTS key; ms === null → PERSIST; else PEXPIRE key ms.

steps.title: The user sees the result
steps.detail: A message confirms the new expiry and the tree or grid refreshes.
steps.tech: showInformationMessage; tree.refresh() in finally; the grid re-runs runPreview.

checks.question: How do you make an expiring key permanent?
checks.answer: Enter 0 or leave the box blank, or press Persist in the grid toolbar.

journeys.title: A user deletes a Redis key
journeys.trigger: Right-clicks a key (or its trash icon) and chooses Delete Key
journeys.summary: A modal confirmation names the key and its database and warns it cannot be undone; on confirm the whole key is removed and the tree refreshes.
rules: Deleting a key always asks first, naming the key and the database.
The deletion cannot be undone.
Only the tree's Delete Key removes a whole key; deleting a row in the grid removes just that element.
A failure is shown as an error message, never ignored.

steps.title: The user chooses Delete Key
steps.detail: It is on the key's right-click menu and as an inline trash icon.
steps.tech: openDbClient.deleteKey when viewItem == key (inline@0 and 9_danger@1).

steps.title: A modal asks for confirmation
steps.detail: It names the key and database and says the deletion cannot be undone.
steps.tech: showWarningMessage(..., { modal: true }, 'Delete'); anything but 'Delete' returns.

steps.title: Redis deletes the whole key
steps.detail: The command passes no element, which tells the driver to remove the entire key.
steps.tech: driver.deleteRow(nodePath, {}) → SELECT db; DEL key.

steps.title: The tree refreshes
steps.detail: Success or failure is reported and the key list is redrawn.
steps.tech: showInformationMessage / showErrorMessage; tree.refresh() in finally.

checks.question: Can deleting a row in the key's grid wipe the whole key?
checks.answer: No. The grid always names the element, so only that element is removed. Only Delete Key in the tree removes the whole key.

journeys.title: A contributor adds a new database engine
journeys.trigger: Wants the extension to support another database
