journeys.summary: A new engine is one driver file implementing the shared driver interface plus one case in the registry; the tree, query panel and commands then work with it unchanged. In practice a few small lists elsewhere must also learn the new type.
rules: The tree, query panel and commands must never import a database library directly; only the new driver does.
Capabilities the engine lacks are left out, not faked: no pretend cancel, row count or expiry.
Table, schema and column names in generated SQL must go through the quoting helpers; values must always be parameters.
Anything that shows less than everything must say so.
Pure helpers are exported from the driver and covered by plain Node tests.

steps.title: Write one driver file
steps.detail: Implement every required method of the driver interface and return results in the shared result shape.
steps.tech: class XDriver implements Driver { connect(secrets), dispose, children(path, filter?), query(sql, database?, token?), previewTable, foreignKeys, schemaHints, tableColumns, getDDL, updateCell, deleteRow, insertRow }.

steps.title: Leave out what the engine cannot do
steps.detail: Optional members are omitted rather than stubbed, and callers already guard for them.
steps.tech: cancel?(token), canCancel (true only for real server-side stop), countRows?, setTtl?. Athena omits countRows; SQLite omits cancel.

steps.title: Quote every identifier
steps.detail: Use the shared quoting helpers for names and pass values as parameters.
steps.tech: quoteIdent / quoteBacktick, or an engine-local quoter as Athena does (q for Trino DML, qDdl for Hive DDL).

steps.title: Add the registry case
steps.detail: One switch case maps the new connection type to the new driver.
steps.tech: createDriver(): case 'x': return new XDriver(config). If the tree path does not start with the database, teach databaseFromPath().

refs.label: Athena blueprint scope: one driver file, one registry case

steps.title: Register the type with the rest of the app
steps.detail: Add the type to the connection type list, a form section for its fields, an icon pair, a display name and, for SQL engines, a dialect.
steps.tech: DatabaseType union + DEFAULT_PORTS (Record, so the compiler forces it); portability TYPES; DIALECTS; describe(); media/icons/<type>.svg and <type>-connected.svg; connectionFormPanel section. Never rename a persisted field.

steps.title: Test the pure helpers
steps.detail: Export the driver's pure functions and test them with Node's built-in runner against the compiled output.
steps.tech: npm test → tsc to out/ → node --test test/*.test.js; import from ../out/drivers/x.js.

checks.question: Is a registry case really the only change outside the driver file?
checks.answer: No. The type also has to be added to the type list, the import/export list, the form, the icons, the tree's display name and, for SQL, the dialect map.

journeys.title: A user queries and edits a SQLite file
journeys.trigger: Connects to a saved SQLite connection and runs a statement or edits a cell
journeys.summary: The whole file is loaded into memory through WebAssembly when the connection opens; every change is applied in memory and then the entire file is rewritten on disk straight away.
rules: The file must exist when connecting; nothing is created for you.
Any statement that does not start with SELECT, and every grid edit, rewrites the whole file on disk.
Changes made to the file by another program after connecting are not seen, and are overwritten by the next write.
A running SQLite statement cannot be stopped, so no Abort button is shown.

steps.title: The file is read into memory
steps.detail: Connecting reads the whole file and opens it with the WebAssembly build of SQLite.
steps.tech: fs.readFileSync(filePath) → new SQL.Database(buffer); sql.js located via setSqliteWasmDir(dist/).

steps.title: The tree lists tables directly
steps.detail: There is no database or schema level; tables and views are the top level.
steps.tech: sqlite_master WHERE type IN ('table','view'); folders via PRAGMA index_list/foreign_key_list/table_info.

steps.title: A statement runs in memory
steps.detail: It runs to completion on the extension's main thread; nothing else can happen until it finishes.
steps.tech: this.d.exec(sql) is synchronous WASM; no cancel() is implemented.

steps.title: The panel hides the Abort button
steps.detail: Because the statement cannot be interrupted, no button that would do nothing is offered.
steps.tech: abortCaps.canAbort = typeof driver.cancel === 'function' → false for SQLite.

steps.title: Changes are written back to the file
steps.detail: After any non-SELECT statement or grid edit, the whole in-memory database is exported over the original file.
steps.tech: persist(): fs.writeFileSync(filePath, Buffer.from(db.export())); triggered when !/^\s*select/i.test(sql).

checks.question: If another app writes to the .db file while it is open here, what happens?
checks.answer: This extension does not see that change, and its next write replaces the whole file with its own in-memory copy.

journeys.title: A user runs a query on Athena
journeys.trigger: Writes SQL in a query panel on an Athena connection and presses Run
journeys.summary: The query is started in the connection's workgroup, checked until it finishes, and its rows are read page by page; the footer shows how much data it scanned, because that is what Athena bills.
rules: Every run is billed for the data it scans, and the footer shows that amount.
A failed or cancelled run still reports what it scanned, since it is still billed.
Abort really stops the query on Athena; closing the connection does not, so a finished result is not thrown away.
The grid holds at most 10,000 rows and says so; reading those rows scans nothing extra.
Browsing, autocomplete and DDL use free catalog lookups, never a billed query.

steps.title: The query is started in the workgroup
steps.detail: It is sent with the workgroup, catalog, database and, unless the workgroup enforces its own, the results location.
steps.tech: StartQueryExecution { QueryString, WorkGroup, QueryExecutionContext {Catalog, Database}, ResultConfiguration? }; output location resolved once at connect via GetWorkGroup.

steps.title: The driver checks until it finishes
steps.detail: It asks for the status quickly at first, then about once a second.
steps.tech: GetQueryExecution poll, 200 ms doubling to 1 s; SUCCEEDED / FAILED / CANCELLED are terminal.

steps.title: A failure says what it cost
steps.detail: A failed or cancelled run reports the reason and the data scanned before stopping.
steps.tech: Error 'Query cancelled: … — you are still billed for the X scanned before it stopped.'

steps.title: Rows are read page by page
steps.detail: Pages are walked up to the grid's 10,000-row limit, reading one extra row so 'there is more' is a fact.
steps.tech: GetQueryResults, ≤ 999 data rows per page (header row detected by stripHeaderRow, compensated by pageSize); MAX_RUN_ROWS = 10,000.

steps.title: The footer shows the cost
steps.detail: Elapsed time and data scanned appear together, with no dollar estimate.
steps.tech: QueryResult.bytesScanned = Statistics.DataScannedInBytes → 'Cost: 2.31s · 1.4 GB scanned'.

steps.title: Abort stops it on Athena
steps.detail: Pressing Abort asks Athena to stop the run; closing the connection deliberately leaves it running.
steps.tech: cancel(token) → StopQueryExecution(running.get(token)); dispose() only clears the map and destroys the client.

checks.question: Does reading more of a large result scan the table again?
checks.answer: No. The rows come from the finished run; reading them scans nothing extra. Only running a new statement is billed again.

journeys.title: A developer writes a query and runs it
journeys.trigger: Opens *New Query* on a connection or database and presses *Run ▶* or Ctrl/Cmd+Enter
journeys.summary: The panel sends the highlighted text, or the whole editor, to the database and shows the rows in the results grid. A long query animates on the Run button and can be stopped with *Abort* where the engine allows it.
rules: With text highlighted only that text runs; otherwise the whole editor runs, and the status line says which.
Only one query runs per panel at a time, and Run stays unavailable until it finishes or is aborted.
PostgreSQL and MySQL stop an aborted query on the server; Redis only stops waiting and says the server may still be working; SQLite shows no Abort button because its engine cannot be interrupted.
A result that arrives after the user aborted is thrown away, and the panel reports *Aborted after 12.4s.* rather than an error.
When the query lock is on, Run refuses and says how to unlock.
The grid paints at most 2,000 rows and says how many it is holding back; export and copy still cover every row.

steps.title: The developer opens a query panel from the tree
steps.detail: The panel is tied to the database the developer picked. A badge in the toolbar names it, and its tooltip repeats the connection's notes.
steps.tech: openDbClient.newQuery → QueryPanel.create({ database: databaseFromPath(type, nodePath) }); contextLabel() / contextTooltip() fill #dbctx; render() emits the CSP'd HTML with a nonce'd script.

steps.title: The panel learns whether this engine can be aborted
steps.detail: It asks the engine once when it opens. The answer decides whether an Abort button exists and what it is called.
steps.tech: advertiseAbort() posts abortCaps { canAbort: typeof driver.cancel === 'function', hard: driver.canCancel === true }; the webview labels the button '■ Abort' or '■ Stop waiting'.

steps.title: Run sends the highlighted text or the whole editor
steps.detail: A locked panel, an empty editor, or a query already running each stop here with a message.
steps.tech: Webview run(): qlock guard → running guard → selection slice → postMessage({ type:'run', sql, seq: ++runSeq }); bound to the Run button and Ctrl/Cmd+Enter.

steps.title: The Run button turns into a live timer
steps.detail: After a short delay the button shows a spinner and the seconds elapsed, so a fast query never flickers. The Abort button appears beside it.
steps.tech: setRunning(true): spinArm = setTimeout(150ms) → makeSpinner(…).start() at 120ms frames; #abortBtn shown when canAbort.

steps.title: The database runs the statement on its own connection
steps.detail: The run is tagged with this panel and run number, so another panel on the same connection is never mixed up with it.
steps.tech: Host run() → driver.query(sql, this.database, runToken(seq)) where token = p<panel>r<seq>; Postgres checks out a pool client and records processID per token in inFlight, released in finally.

steps.title: If the developer aborts, that exact run is cancelled
steps.detail: Pressing *Abort* or Esc tells the server to stop, and the panel stops listening to that run at once. If the server has not stopped after 8 seconds the panel is handed back with a plain warning.
steps.tech: abortRun(): runSeq++ → postMessage abort → handleAbort() sets abortedSeq → driver.cancel?(token) (Postgres SELECT pg_cancel_backend($1), MySQL KILL QUERY <threadId>); aborted() posts { type:'aborted', secs }; abortGuard 8000ms.

steps.title: The grid shows the rows
steps.detail: A stale reply is dropped, the grid paints up to 2,000 rows, and the footer shows the row count and how long it took (and bytes scanned on Athena).
steps.tech: 'result' handler: drop if m.runSeq !== runSeq; setRunning(false); syncColumnsFor; Cost line from elapsedMs / bytesScanned; renderGrid() via cappedView() with RENDER_CAP = 2000 and updateScope().

checks.question: What happens to rows from a query the developer aborted that finished anyway?
checks.answer: They are discarded, and the panel still reports that the query was aborted.

checks.question: Why does a SQLite panel have no Abort button?
checks.answer: SQLite's engine runs inside the extension and cannot be interrupted, so a button there would promise something it cannot do.

journeys.title: Suggestions appear while the developer types SQL
journeys.trigger: Types in the query panel's editor, or presses Ctrl/Cmd+Space
journeys.summary: As the developer types, the panel offers what fits that spot in the statement: tables after FROM, that table's columns after an alias and a dot, and the engine's own keywords and functions. Saved query files get the same suggestions in VS Code's own editor.
rules: Typing never waits on the database and never opens a connection by itself in the query panel; until the connection is live only the engine's keywords, functions and types are offered.
After an alias and a dot, only that table's columns are offered.
Straight after ORDER BY or GROUP BY only columns and functions are offered, so accepting the first suggestion cannot produce invalid SQL.
When the list or the schema was cut short, the list ends with *more matches — keep typing to narrow*.
Esc closes only the list, and Run and Save shortcuts keep working while it is open.
Redis connections get a short list of commands instead of SQL words.

steps.title: Each keystroke asks for suggestions
steps.detail: The panel sends the text up to the caret. Nothing is asked while an input method is composing a character.
steps.tech: acRequest(): postMessage({ type:'complete', text: value.slice(0, selectionStart), seq: ++acSeq }); compositionstart / compositionend suppress it.

steps.title: Table and column names load only from a live connection
steps.detail: They are fetched once per database and remembered. A failed fetch falls back to the engine's vocabulary without showing an error.
steps.tech: ensureHints(): returns early unless manager.isConnected(id); cached per hintsDb; hintsPending guard; driver.schemaHints(database); errors logged only.

steps.title: The suggestion engine works out what fits here
steps.detail: It looks only at the current statement, follows aliases, and decides whether a table, a column or anything belongs at the caret.
steps.tech: suggest(): completionContext() (TABLE_CLAUSES, EXPRESSION_START, qualifier), aliasMap(), currentStatement(), then rank(): exact > prefix > contains, columns > tables > keywords > functions, shorter label first on a typed prefix.

steps.title: Keywords and functions come from the engine's dialect
steps.detail: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and Athena each get their own vocabulary, offline. Redis gets a small fixed command list.
steps.tech: vocabularyFor(type) reads keywords / functions / dataTypes from the sql-formatter dialect's tokenizerOptions; athena → trino; REDIS_COMMANDS static.

steps.title: The list appears at the caret
steps.detail: It opens just below the line being typed, or above it when there is no room. A reply overtaken by newer typing is ignored.
steps.tech: 'completions' handler drops m.seq < acRendered; caretPoint() measures a hidden mirror div minus scrollTop; acRender() flips above when it would clip; listTruncated / schemaTruncated show the 'more matches' row.

steps.title: Accepting replaces only the word being typed
steps.detail: Enter, Tab or a click inserts the suggestion and adds a space only if one is not already there.
steps.tech: acAccept(): walks back over identifier chars, splices the label, adds a trailing space unless the next char is whitespace; keydown handles ↑ ↓ Enter Tab Esc and ignores modified Enter.

steps.title: Saved query files get the same suggestions
steps.detail: Typing in a saved file uses VS Code's own suggestion list, filled by the same engine.
steps.tech: registerSqlFeatures(): CompletionItemProvider on { language:'sql', scheme:'file' }; bindingFor(uri) → hintsFor() (getDriver + schemaHints, cached connId::database) → suggest(…, 400); triggers ' ', '.', ',', '('.

checks.question: What does the developer see before the connection is open?
checks.answer: The engine's keywords, functions and data types, but no table or column names.

checks.question: After typing an alias and a dot, which columns are offered?
checks.answer: Only the columns of the table that alias stands for.

journeys.title: A developer edits a cell in the results grid and saves it
journeys.trigger: Double-clicks a cell, or opens it with 🔍, in a result that can be edited
journeys.summary: A result can be edited only when the extension knows which single table it came from and that table has a primary key. The new value is written back with an update that finds the row by its primary key.
rules: A table preview from the tree can be edited when the table has a primary key.
A typed query can be edited only when it is a plain SELECT from one table, with no joins or unions, and returns every primary-key column; anything else stays read-only.
Tables with no primary key, and every Athena result, are never editable, and nothing falls back to matching rows by their other values.
The new value is sent to the database as a separate parameter, never pasted into the SQL text.
Deleting checked rows asks for confirmation and cannot be undone, and *select all* only reaches rows painted on screen.
While the query lock is on, cell edits, *＋ Row*, *Delete* and TTL changes refuse with a message.

steps.title: The engine decides whether the result is editable
steps.detail: For a preview it looks up the table's primary key; for a typed query it first checks the statement reads from exactly one table.
steps.tech: previewTable sets result.editable = { table, pkColumns } when pkColumns is non-empty; query() → attachEditable(): parseFromTable(sql) → tableColumns() → every PK column must be in result.columns.

steps.title: Editable cells get edit controls
steps.detail: Cells show a 🔍 button, rows get checkboxes, and the status line says *double-click or 🔍 to edit*.
steps.tech: renderGrid(): td.editable + .zoom span + row checkbox column when raw.editable; #addBtn enabled; status suffix at the end of the 'result' handler.

steps.title: The developer types the new value
steps.detail: Enter or clicking away commits; Esc cancels only the edit and never aborts a running query. JSON cells open the JSON viewer instead.
steps.tech: onDblEdit(): jsoncell → openModal; else an input.cell seeded with cellText(original); Enter/blur → commit(); Escape stopPropagation() → renderGrid().

steps.title: The panel sends the row's primary key and the new value
steps.detail: The grid shows the new value straight away while the save is in flight.
steps.tech: saveCell(ri, col, val): qlock guard → pk built from raw.editable.pkColumns → raw.rows[ri][col] = val (optimistic) → postMessage({ type:'update', pk, column, value, rowIndex }).

steps.title: The database applies an update keyed on the primary key
steps.detail: Only the one row whose primary key matches is changed.
steps.tech: handleUpdate() → driver.updateCell(lastEditable.table, pk, column, value) → UPDATE "schema"."table" SET "col" = $1 WHERE "pk" = $2 …, identifiers quoted, values bound.

steps.title: The status line reports the outcome
steps.detail: It reads *Updated* and the column name, or *Update failed* with the database's message. On failure the cell keeps showing the typed value until the grid is refreshed.
steps.tech: Host posts updateResult { ok, message }; the webview only sets statusEl text, it does not roll back raw.rows.

checks.question: Why can a JOIN result not be edited?
checks.answer: The extension cannot tell which table a changed cell belongs to, so the grid stays read-only instead of guessing.

checks.question: How is the row to change identified?
checks.answer: By the values of its primary-key columns, which is why a table without a primary key cannot be edited.

journeys.title: A developer follows a foreign key to the related row
journeys.trigger: Clicks ↗ on a linked cell in a table preview
journeys.summary: In a table preview, columns that point at another table show their values as links. Clicking ↗ opens a new panel on the referenced table, filtered to the matching row.
rules: Links appear only in table previews opened from the tree, where the engine has looked up the table's foreign keys; typed queries show none.
The new panel is a full preview with typed headers, paging and, if that table has a primary key, editing.
The value being followed is sent to the database as a parameter, and the editor shows an equivalent statement to read.
If the column has no foreign key after all, a warning says so and nothing opens.

steps.title: A preview carries the table's foreign keys
steps.detail: Along with the rows, the engine reports which columns reference which table and column.
steps.tech: previewTable() sets result.foreignKeys = await this.foreignKeys(path) (information_schema lookup) and columnsMeta with fk markers.

steps.title: Linked cells are drawn as links
steps.detail: The value gets a dotted link style and a ↗ button that appears on hover.
steps.tech: renderGrid(): fkCols from raw.foreignKeys → td.fkcell, span.fkval, span.relbtn[data-col].

steps.title: Clicking ↗ asks for the related row
steps.detail: The panel sends the column and the cell's value to the extension.
steps.tech: wireGrid(): .relbtn click → postMessage({ type:'openRelated', column, value: raw.rows[ri][col] }).

steps.title: A new panel opens on the referenced table
steps.detail: It is a fresh preview of that table with an equality filter on the referenced column.
steps.tech: openRelated(): find fk in lastResult.foreignKeys → QueryPanel.create({ previewPath: fk.refTable, filter: { column: fk.refColumn, value } }).

steps.title: The database returns the matching rows
steps.detail: The filter runs as a bound parameter, and the editor is filled with a readable version of the statement.
steps.tech: runPreview() → previewTable(path, { filter }) → buildWhere pushes "col" = $n; result.sql = displaySql(…) replaces the editor text on 'result'.

checks.question: Do foreign-key links appear on a hand-typed query?
checks.answer: No. They appear only on table previews opened from the tree.

journeys.title: A developer inspects a JSON cell and narrows the visible columns
journeys.trigger: Clicks ⤢ on a JSON cell, or opens *Columns ▾*
journeys.summary: A JSON value shows as a short summary in the grid and opens in a collapsible tree with a *Raw* tab. The column picker hides columns from view, and everything that follows the screen says so.
rules: Any cell holding a JSON object or array, or text that reads as one, gets the viewer, on any result including joins and views.
The tree is read-only; editing happens on the *Raw* tab, and only when the result is editable.
Each expansion shows at most 1,000 children and says how many it held back; documents over about 2 MB open on *Raw* with an explanation.
The button reads *Columns 5/9* whenever anything is hidden, and the last visible column cannot be hidden.
Hiding a column clears its filter and says so; search, *Copy as JSON* and export follow the visible columns, while *＋ Row* still lists every column.
Column choices last while the panel is open, survive re-running the same query, and reset when different columns come back.

steps.title: JSON cells show a summary chip
steps.detail: Instead of a wall of text the cell reads, for example, *{…} 12 keys*. Dates and binary values are not mistaken for JSON.
steps.tech: jsonShape(v) in JSON_VIEW_HELPERS (objects/arrays, or strings that trim to { or [ and JSON.parse; excludes Date and ArrayBuffer views) → jsonSummary(); renderGrid adds td.jsoncell + ⤢ regardless of editable.

steps.title: The viewer opens on a tree
steps.detail: Nodes deeper than two levels start collapsed and expand on click. Values are written as plain text, never as markup.
steps.tech: openModal(): JSON_TREE_MAX_CHARS (2 MB) → Raw with a note; else buildNode() lazily, JSON_NODE_CAP = 1000 children per expansion; text nodes only, escAttr where an attribute is unavoidable.

steps.title: The developer copies a value or its path
steps.detail: Each node can copy its value or a path such as *$.items[3].sku*; very large copies ask first.
steps.tech: copyBtn() → postMessage({ type:'copy', text }) → handleCopy() with the COPY_WARN_CHARS (5 MB) modal.

steps.title: Edits are saved from the Raw tab
steps.detail: Save is switched off on the tree and on results that cannot be edited.
steps.tech: showTab(): msave.disabled = tree || !raw.editable; #msave → saveCell(ri, col, textEl.value); the engine casts the bound string to jsonb.

steps.title: The column picker hides and shows columns
steps.detail: A searchable checklist with *Show all* and *Hide all*; hiding a filtered column drops that filter and says so.
steps.tech: renderColsMenu() (last visible checkbox locked), toggleColumn() deletes filters[c] and re-posts 'filter' when server-backed, syncColsBtn() label 'Columns n/m'.

steps.title: A different result starts with every column shown
steps.detail: Re-running the same query keeps the choice; a new set of columns resets it.
steps.tech: syncColumnsFor(result): columnsKey(result.columns) compared with colsKey; mismatch → hidden = new Set().

checks.question: Can a JSON value from a JOIN be inspected?
checks.answer: Yes. The viewer works on any result; only saving an edit needs an editable result.

checks.question: Does hiding a column change an export?
checks.answer: Yes. Export writes only the visible columns and the confirmation says how many of the total it kept.

journeys.title: A developer exports results to CSV or JSON
journeys.trigger: Clicks *Export CSV*, *Export JSON* or *Copy as JSON* in the results bar
journeys.summary: Export writes the last result to a file the developer picks; *Copy as JSON* puts rows on the clipboard. Both use the visible columns, and both cover rows beyond the 2,000 the grid paints.
rules: Export covers every row the last query returned, including rows past the 2,000 painted in the grid.
On a paged table preview, only the loaded page is in the result, and the confirmation gives the row count it wrote.
Hidden columns are left out, and the confirmation says *5 of 9 columns* when that happens.
CSV quotes values containing commas, quotes or line breaks, and writes JSON values as JSON text rather than *[object Object]*.
*Copy as JSON* copies the checked rows, or every row in view when none are checked, in the grid's current order and filters; one checked row copies as a single object.
A clipboard payload over 5 MB asks before copying.

steps.title: The panel sends which columns are visible
steps.detail: The export request names the columns on screen.
steps.tech: #csvBtn / #jsonBtn → postMessage({ type:'export', format, columns: cols() }); an absent columns list means all.

steps.title: The extension narrows the last result to those columns
steps.detail: Unknown column names are ignored rather than invented, so the file never fills with blanks.
steps.tech: handleExport() → projectResult(lastResult, columns) keeps result order and every row's keys.

steps.title: The developer picks where to save
steps.detail: VS Code's own save dialog opens, filtered to CSV or JSON.
steps.tech: vscode.window.showSaveDialog({ filters, saveLabel: 'Export CSV' | 'Export JSON' }).

steps.title: The file is written and the count reported
steps.detail: The message gives the number of rows, the columns kept if any were hidden, and the path.
steps.tech: toCsv(result) or JSON.stringify(result.rows, null, 2) → fs.writeFileSync(uri.fsPath) → showInformationMessage('Exported N row(s), a of b columns to …').

steps.title: Copy as JSON goes to the clipboard
steps.detail: Rows follow the grid's sort, filters, search and visible columns.
steps.tech: copyAsJson(): computeView() → selected subset or all → projectRows(…, cols()) → postMessage copy → handleCopy() with COPY_WARN_CHARS confirm → vscode.env.clipboard.writeText.

checks.question: Does an export include rows the grid did not paint?
checks.answer: Yes. Painting stops at 2,000 rows, but export uses the whole last result.

journeys.title: A developer saves a query as a file and runs it later
journeys.trigger: Uses + on the *Query* node under a database to add a file or folder, then *Run Query File* or the ▶ Run lens
journeys.summary: Saved queries are ordinary .sql files kept in the extension's own storage, grouped per connection and database and listed in the tree under *Query*. They open in VS Code's editor with suggestions, formatting and a ▶ Run lens on each statement.
rules: Files live in the extension's storage on this machine, not in the project folder, and *Reset All Data* removes them all.
*Run Query File* runs the whole file as last saved to disk; the ▶ Run lens runs only the statement it sits on.
Results open in one reusable results panel per connection; *{ } JSON* opens the rows as a JSON document instead.
Deleting a file or folder asks first and skips the bin, so it cannot be undone.
File and folder names are reduced to safe characters before they reach the disk.

steps.title: The tree shows a Query folder under each database
steps.detail: It lists sub-folders first, then .sql files, or a hint to add one when empty.
steps.tech: queryRootNode() adds an '@queries' node (contextValue queryroot); queryChildNodes() → splitQueryPath() → queries.list(connId, scope, relative).

steps.title: A new file is created on disk
steps.detail: The developer names it, and it is written with a comment header and opened as SQL.
steps.tech: openDbClient.newQueryFile → queries.createFile() writes '-- <name>' under <globalStorage>/queries/<connId>@@<db>[@<schema>]/…/<name>.sql (encodeKey + san()).

steps.title: The file opens in VS Code's editor, tied to its connection
steps.detail: The extension remembers which connection and database the file belongs to, and can work it out from the file's folder after a restart.
steps.tech: openDbClient.openQueryFile → bindQueryDoc(uri, connId, scope[0]); fallback QueryStore.resolveUri() → parseKey(first folder segment).

steps.title: Each statement gets a Run lens
steps.detail: The file is split at each semicolon, and every statement gets ▶ Run and { } JSON above it.
steps.tech: CodeLensProvider: splitStatements() splits on every ';' → openDbClient.runSql / runSqlJson with [connId, database, stmt.text].

steps.title: Running shows results in the reusable panel
steps.detail: The first run opens a results panel for the connection; later runs reuse it and replace its SQL.
steps.tech: runQueryFile reads the file via queries.read(); runSql / runQueryFile → QueryPanel.runInResults() → existing.rerun(sql, database) (host run() directly) or a new panel with autoRun.

steps.title: Deleting removes it for good
steps.detail: A confirmation names the file or folder, then it is deleted without going to the bin.
steps.tech: openDbClient.deleteQueryFile / deleteQueryFolder modal → queries.delete(uri) with { recursive: true, useTrash: false }.

checks.question: Does *Run Query File* include edits that are not saved yet?
checks.answer: No. It reads the file from disk, so unsaved changes are not run.

checks.question: Where are saved query files kept?
checks.answer: In the extension's own storage folder on this machine, one folder per connection and database.

journeys.title: A query panel is locked against running and editing
journeys.actor: Developer, or the AI assistant on their behalf
journeys.trigger: Clicks 🔓 in the toolbar, or the AI generates or fixes SQL that writes
journeys.summary: The query lock makes one panel read-only: nothing runs and nothing in the grid changes until someone clicks the lock again. It turns itself on when the AI produces a write, so the habitual Ctrl/Cmd+Enter after *Generate* cannot run it unreviewed.
rules: Locked, the panel refuses Run, Ctrl/Cmd+Enter, highlight-to-run, cell edits, *＋ Row*, *Delete* and TTL changes, each with the same message.
AI output that inserts, updates, deletes, merges, replaces or changes the schema locks the panel by itself, and the note line says which verb; *Explain* never locks.
SQL the developer typed never locks the panel by itself.
One click unlocks, whether the lock was set by hand or by the AI.
Unlocking while a query is running does not hand Run back until that query ends.
The lock belongs to one open panel and is forgotten when the panel closes.

steps.title: The developer toggles the lock
steps.detail: The button shows 🔒 or 🔓 and the status line says what changed.
steps.tech: #lockBtn → setLock(!qlock); runBtn.disabled = on || running; .locked styling.

steps.title: AI output is checked for writes
steps.detail: Every statement in the generated SQL is scanned for a writing verb, including writes wrapped in a WITH clause.
steps.tech: handleAi() → AiService.run() returns mutation: isMutation(sql) (comment-strip, split on ';', leading verb in INSERT…CREATE, WITH + embedded write) → aiResult.mutation.

steps.title: A write engages the lock
steps.detail: The note under the editor reads *🔒 auto-locked (UPDATE) — unlock to run*.
steps.tech: 'aiResult' handler: if (m.mutation && m.verb !== 'explain') setLock(true) and prefix the note.

steps.title: Every blocked action says why
steps.detail: Run, cell saves, row delete, the add-row form and TTL buttons each stop with *Query lock is on — click the lock to unlock*.
steps.tech: lockNudge() guards in run(), saveCell(), deleteSelected(), openAddModal(), #ttlEdit and #ttlPersist; all webview-side.

checks.question: Does typing an UPDATE by hand lock the panel?
checks.answer: No. Only SQL the AI generated or fixed engages the lock by itself.

checks.question: How does a developer unlock a panel the AI locked?
checks.answer: One click on the lock button, the same as a lock set by hand.

journeys.title: A user sets up an AI provider in Settings
journeys.trigger: Opens Settings & Guides, then the AI Assistant section
journeys.summary: The user picks a provider, pastes their own API key and tests it. The key goes to the operating system's keychain, and the assist bar appears in query panels once setup is complete.
rules: The user brings their own key; requests go straight from their machine to their provider, with nothing of ours in between.
The key is kept in the operating system's keychain, never in settings files, connection exports or logs.
Leaving the key field blank on save keeps the stored key; it never deletes it.
Local providers such as Ollama on this machine need no key.
AI can be switched off for any single connection, and that takes effect in query panels that are already open.
Consent to send schema names can be revoked at any time; the next request asks again.

steps.title: The user opens the AI Assistant section
steps.detail: Settings & Guides opens as its own tab with a guide for each topic.
steps.tech: Command `openDbClient.settings` → `SettingsPanel.open(ctx)`; the AI form is rendered by the `ai-assistant` guide and filled from an `aiState` message.

steps.title: The user picks a preset
steps.detail: Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, OpenRouter or a custom compatible endpoint; the base URL and a default model fill in, and each provider remembers what it was last saved with.
steps.tech: `AI_PRESETS` in `registry.ts`; per-provider form memory in `AiSettings.perProvider`.

steps.title: The key is saved to the keychain
steps.detail: Settings go to the extension's stored state; the key goes to the operating system's keychain under that provider's name.
steps.tech: `aiSave` → `saveAiForm` → `AiStore.update` (globalState `openDbClient.ai`) and `AiStore.setKey` (SecretStorage `openDbClient.aiKey.<providerId>`).

steps.title: The user fetches the live model list
steps.detail: The ↻ button lists the models the endpoint serves right now, with a price next to each where one is known.
steps.tech: `aiFetchModels` → `AiService.listModels`: endpoint prices first, else the price table or LiteLLM mirror, shown with a `~`.

steps.title: The user presses Test
steps.detail: A one-word request proves the key, endpoint and model work, and reports how long it took or a readable reason it failed.
steps.tech: `aiTest` saves the on-screen form first, then `AiService.test` sends a ping with a 512-token cap; failures come back as `AiError` messages from `normalizeHttpError`. The call is recorded in the ledger with verb `test`.

steps.title: Open query panels show the assist bar
steps.detail: Once setup is complete every SQL query panel shows the assist bar; Redis panels never do.
steps.tech: `notifyAiSettingsChanged()` → each panel's `syncAiBar()` posts `aiEnabled` when `isConfigured()` and `enabledFor(connId)` and the engine is not Redis.

steps.title: The user can switch AI off for a connection
steps.detail: Unticking a connection removes the assist bar from its query panels at once, even ones already open beside Settings.
steps.tech: `aiSetConnEnabled` → `AiStore.setAiEnabledFor` (adds to `disabledConnections`) → `notifyAiSettingsChanged()` → `syncAiBar()` posts `aiDisabled`. Fixed in 1.4.2.

checks.question: Where does the API key end up after Save?
checks.answer: In the operating system's keychain, filed under that provider. Settings such as the base URL and model are kept separately.

checks.question: A user unticks a connection while its query panel is open beside Settings. What happens?
checks.answer: The assist bar disappears from that panel straight away, without reopening it.

checks.question: Does Ollama on this machine need a key?
checks.answer: No. The preset needs no key, so setup is complete with a base URL and a model.

journeys.title: A user generates SQL from a plain-English request
journeys.trigger: Types what they want into the assist bar and presses Generate
journeys.summary: The extension sends the request, the current query and the connected database's table and column names to the user's AI provider, then puts the returned SQL into the editor for review. It never runs it.
rules: Only the request, the query in the editor, earlier requests in that panel, schema names, types and foreign-key links, and the dialect are sent; row data and query results never are.
The first request to a remote provider asks for consent; local endpoints skip the question.
On a large database the schema sent is cut down to the tables the request names plus their direct links, and the bar says so.
Generated SQL is placed in the editor selected and is never run automatically.
Dangerous statements get a visible warning, and any statement that writes data locks the editor until the user unlocks it.
Every call shows its time, size and estimated cost; a model with no known price shows no cost rather than zero.

steps.title: The user asks in plain English
steps.detail: Table and column names autocomplete in the request box while they type.
steps.tech: Webview posts `{ type: 'ai', verb: 'generate', prompt, sql, seq }`; `handleAi` adds the panel's last six Generate prompts as history. Identifier suggestions come from `aiComplete`.

steps.title: The opt-out and consent are checked
steps.detail: A connection with AI switched off is refused; otherwise the first request to a remote provider asks once what may be sent.
steps.tech: `AiService.run` → `aiEnabledFor(connId)`, then `ensureConsent()`: a modal naming the host unless `consentGiven` or `isLocalBaseUrl(baseUrl)`.

steps.title: The schema is read from the connection
steps.detail: Table names, column names and types come from the live connection, plus foreign-key links for the tables involved.
steps.tech: `driver.schemaHints(database)`; `collectFks` calls `driver.foreignKeys` for referenced tables, at most 20, tolerating failures.

steps.title: The schema context is built within a budget
steps.detail: The whole schema goes when it fits; otherwise the tables the request or current query names plus one foreign-key hop, cut further if needed.
steps.tech: `buildSchemaContext(focus, schema, 6000)` with the chars/4 `estimateTokens` guard; `trimmed: true` and the kept table count travel back as `trimmedTo`.

steps.title: The prompt pins the dialect and the house rules
steps.detail: The model is told the exact engine, to use only the given tables, to write one runnable statement, and not to write destructive SQL unless asked.
steps.tech: `systemPrompt('generate', connType)` with `RUNNABLE_RULES` (no bind parameters; a leading `params` CTE) and `STYLE_RULES`; `generateUserPrompt(intent, ctx.text, currentSql, history)`.

steps.title: The request goes to the user's provider
steps.detail: One request from this machine to the configured endpoint with the user's own key.
steps.tech: `createAiProvider(config).complete({ system, user, maxTokens: 4096 }, key)` → `POST /v1/messages` (Anthropic) or `POST {base}/chat/completions`.

steps.title: Usage is recorded and the cost estimated
steps.detail: The exact counts from the reply go into the local ledger; a new model gets a price row before the estimate is made.
steps.tech: `UsageStore.record`, then `autoPrice(providerId, res.model)`, then `estimateCost(..., findPrice(...))`.

steps.title: The SQL is pulled out and checked
steps.detail: The statement is taken from the reply and tagged when it drops, truncates or alters, deletes or updates without a filter, or writes at all.
steps.tech: `extractSql`, `isDestructive`, `isMutation` (token scans, fail-safe).

steps.title: The SQL lands in the editor for review
steps.detail: It is inserted selected, with the explanation, any warning, lock or trim notice, and the time, size and estimated cost of the call.
steps.tech: `aiResult` handler: follow-ups replace the AI's own last output, otherwise `aiInsertSql`; `destructive` → ⚠ tag; `mutation` → `setLock(true)`; `trimmedTo` → trim notice; meta line `✓ 2.1s · N tokens · ~$… · model (provider)`.

checks.question: Does the provider ever see rows from the database?
checks.answer: No. It gets the request, the query in the editor, earlier requests in that panel, schema names and types, foreign-key links and the dialect.

checks.question: What happens on a database with thousands of tables?
checks.answer: Only the tables the request or current query names, plus their direct links, are sent, and the bar says the schema was trimmed and to how many tables.

checks.question: The model returns an UPDATE with no WHERE. Can Ctrl+Enter run it straight away?
checks.answer: No. It is tagged as dangerous and, because it writes, the editor locks until the user unlocks it.

journeys.title: A user checks their AI usage and estimated cost
journeys.trigger: Opens Settings & Guides → AI Assistant after using the assist bar
journeys.summary: Every AI call is counted on the user's machine from the provider's exact figures. Cost is an estimate from fetched prices, worked out each time the tables are shown, and is never invented.
rules: Usage is counted locally and never reported anywhere.
No price ships with the extension; every price is fetched from the provider or the LiteLLM community list and labelled with its source.
A model with no price shows '—', and a total that includes one is marked as partial.
A price older than 30 days, or one whose source could not be reached, is marked stale but still used.
Live account balances are not shown; the user checks their provider's dashboard.
Past usage is costed at today's prices, so refreshing a price re-costs history.

steps.title: Each call adds one usage record
steps.detail: Time, provider, the model the server reported, the action and exact token counts; the oldest records drop after 5,000, but all-time totals stay exact.
steps.tech: `applyRecord` appends, trims to `USAGE_CAP`, bumps `dropped` and `totals[provider␀model␀verb]`; stored under globalState `openDbClient.aiUsage`.

steps.title: A new model is priced on first use
steps.detail: The provider's own published price wins; otherwise the local LiteLLM copy, downloaded once if it is empty.
steps.tech: `autoPrice` runs only when `findPrice` misses; `listModelsFor` then `lookupLitellm` via `ensureLitellmTable()`; failures leave the model unpriced.

steps.title: Settings shows the usage tables
steps.detail: Current period and all time, per provider, model and action, with tokens and estimated cost.
steps.tech: `postAiState` → `summarizePeriod` / `summarizeAllTime` with a `findPrice` lookup; the webview renders '—' and a `+?` total for unpriced rows.

steps.title: The trend chart shows the last 30 days
steps.detail: Daily stacked bars by provider or model, tokens or estimated cost; calls with no price are counted and left out of the cost view.
steps.tech: `usageTrend(state, lookup, groupBy, now)` buckets UTC days host-side, top six series plus 'other'.

steps.title: The user refreshes or adds prices
steps.detail: Refresh re-reads every row from its own source and removes models no longer priced; Price used models fills gaps from the history; Update price list re-downloads LiteLLM.
steps.tech: `aiRefreshPrices` → `refreshPrices` (`mergeFetched` / `mergeLitellm`, offline for LiteLLM rows); `aiPriceFromUsage` → `addPricesFromUsage`; `aiRefreshLitellm` → `refreshLitellmTable` (keeps the old table on failure).

steps.title: The price list is fetched from outside
steps.detail: Provider model lists, and the LiteLLM community file on GitHub for providers that publish no prices.
steps.tech: `GET {base}/models` or `/v1/models`; `fetch(LITELLM_PRICES_URL)` parsed by `parseLitellmTable` into ~129 KB of tuples.

steps.title: The user can reset the period or erase everything
steps.detail: Reset period starts a new current period without touching all-time totals; Reset all data removes the ledger, prices, AI settings and keys.
steps.tech: `aiResetPeriod` → `UsageStore.resetPeriod`; `openDbClient.resetAllData` → `AiStore.deleteAll` + `UsageStore.deleteAll`.

checks.question: Is the cost shown in Settings what the provider will bill?
checks.answer: No. It is an estimate from exact usage figures times fetched list prices; the provider's dashboard is the bill.

checks.question: A model's price row was removed with ✕. What happens the next time it is used?
checks.answer: It is priced again automatically, so ✕ hides the row only until that model is used again.

checks.question: Why might an old month's cost change?
checks.answer: Costs are not stored; they are worked out from today's price table, so a refreshed price re-costs history.

journeys.title: Brian releases and publishes a new version
journeys.trigger: Runs npm run release:patch (or minor/major) on a clean main
journeys.summary: A release bumps the version, turns the Unreleased notes into a dated changelog section, tags and packages locally. Publishing is a separate step that ships that same package to the Marketplace and Open VSX and only then pushes.
rules: Every change gets a version bump, patch at minimum; a number is never reused or skipped.
Releases are cut only through the release scripts, never by the Marketplace tool's own bump, so the changelog stays in step.
Publishing refuses a dirty tree or a version with no dated changelog section.
One package file is built and sent to both registries.
Nothing is pushed until a publish succeeds; until then a bad release can be undone locally.
A failed GitHub release page does not count as a failed publish.

steps.title: Notes collect under Unreleased
steps.detail: Each change adds a line to the top section of the changelog while work is in progress.
steps.tech: `## [Unreleased]` in `CHANGELOG.md` (Keep a Changelog).

steps.title: The release command runs the tests first
steps.detail: A failing test stops the release before anything changes.
steps.tech: `release:patch` = `npm version patch && npm run package`; `preversion: npm test`. `npm version` also refuses a dirty working tree.

steps.title: The changelog is stamped with the new version
steps.detail: The Unreleased notes become a dated section for the new number, and a fresh empty Unreleased section is left on top.
steps.tech: `version` hook → `scripts/stamp-changelog.mjs` (idempotent; aborts with no Unreleased marker) → `git add CHANGELOG.md`; npm then commits and tags `vX.Y.Z`.

steps.title: The package is built
steps.detail: A typecheck and a minified production bundle run before the package file is written.
steps.tech: `npm run package` → `vsce package` → `vscode:prepublish` (`typecheck` + `bundle -- --production`).

steps.title: Publishing checks the release state
steps.detail: It refuses a dirty tree or a version without a dated changelog section, and warns if the tag is missing.
steps.tech: `publish:marketplace` → `assertReleasedState()`; with `--ovsx`, `OVSX_PAT` must be set before anything is published.

steps.title: One package goes to both registries
steps.detail: The package is built once and that same file is uploaded to the Marketplace, then to Open VSX.
steps.tech: `packageVsix` → `vsce publish --packagePath <file>`; `ovsx publish <file>` when `--ovsx`. `publish:ovsx` alone refuses a version Open VSX already has and warns about an unverified namespace.

steps.title: The release is pushed and a GitHub release cut
steps.detail: Only now are the commit and tag pushed; the GitHub release takes its notes from the changelog and a failure there is only a warning.
steps.tech: `git push && git push --tags` (skip with `--no-push`), then `scripts/github-release.mjs` via `cutGithubRelease()`.

steps.title: Brian confirms what is live
steps.detail: A check compares the live versions with the local one and says when Open VSX is holding an upload inactive.
steps.tech: `marketplace:verify [-- --ovsx]` → public gallery API and Open VSX API; non-zero exit on drift.

checks.question: Brian bumps the version with the Marketplace tool directly. What breaks?
checks.answer: The changelog is not stamped, so the version and changelog fall out of step, and the publish script then refuses it.

checks.question: When does the release tag reach GitHub?
checks.answer: Only after a successful publish; the release command itself pushes nothing.

checks.question: Do Cursor users get a different build from VS Code users?
checks.answer: No. One package file is built and the same file is uploaded to both registries.

journeys.title: A contributor runs the tests
journeys.trigger: Runs npm test, or a release runs it automatically
journeys.summary: The TypeScript source is compiled to a plain output folder and Node's built-in test runner checks the pure logic there. Anything needing the editor itself is checked by hand.
rules: Tests cover pure logic only; nothing in them starts VS Code.
A function under test must be exported from its source file.
Provider adapters are tested against a fake network, never a real provider.
A failing test blocks a release.
Behaviour inside the editor is checked by hand against the QA checklists.

steps.title: The source is compiled
steps.detail: TypeScript compiles every source file into a separate output folder that the tests load.
steps.tech: `npm test` → `npm run compile` (`tsc -p ./`, `outDir: out`, CommonJS, ES2021).

steps.title: Node runs every test file
steps.detail: Each test file loads the compiled modules it checks and asserts on their behaviour.
steps.tech: `node --test test/*.test.js`; files `require('../out/...')` and use `node:test` / `node:assert`.

steps.title: AI adapters are tested with a fake network
steps.detail: Replies, usage figures and error messages are checked against canned responses.
steps.tech: `createAiProvider(config, mockFetch(status, body))` — `FetchLike` is injectable.

steps.title: Editor behaviour is checked by hand
steps.detail: F5 builds the bundle and opens a second VS Code window with the extension loaded, where the QA checklists are run.
steps.tech: `.vscode/launch.json` *Run Extension* with `preLaunchTask: npm: bundle`; checklists in `docs/TESTING.md` and task.md QA gates.

checks.question: Can a test call the VS Code API?
checks.answer: No. Tests load compiled modules outside the editor, so they cover pure logic only.

checks.question: Do the AI adapter tests need an API key?
checks.answer: No. They use a fake network that returns canned replies.

journeys.title: A contributor commits and the secret scan runs
journeys.trigger: Runs git commit
journeys.summary: Before every commit the staged files are auto-formatted, then gitleaks scans the whole history and the staged change for secrets. Without gitleaks installed the commit is refused.
rules: Every commit is scanned for secrets, both the change being committed and all existing history.
Findings are printed redacted, so the scan never prints the secret it found.
If gitleaks is not installed the commit is refused rather than going in unscanned.
Staged files are auto-formatted and safe lint fixes applied before the scan.

steps.title: The hook starts
steps.detail: The pre-commit hook installed on npm install runs before the commit is recorded.
steps.tech: `prepare: husky` installs `.husky/pre-commit`.

steps.title: Staged files are formatted
steps.detail: Biome fixes formatting and safe lint issues in just the files being committed.
steps.tech: `npx lint-staged` → `biome check --write --no-errors-on-unmatched` on `*.{ts,js,mjs,json,jsonc}`.

steps.title: The scan refuses to run blind
steps.detail: With no gitleaks on the machine the commit stops with an install hint.
steps.tech: `command -v gitleaks` or exit 1.

steps.title: History and the staged change are scanned
steps.detail: One pass over every committed branch, one over the change about to be committed, both redacted.
steps.tech: `gitleaks detect --source . --log-opts="--all" --redact`, then `gitleaks git --pre-commit --staged --redact .`; `set -e` aborts on a finding.

checks.question: Why two scans?
checks.answer: A history scan cannot see what is not committed yet, so the staged change gets its own pass.

checks.question: What happens on a new laptop without gitleaks?
checks.answer: The commit is refused with a hint to install it.

glossary.definition: One saved way to reach a database: a server (PostgreSQL, MySQL/MariaDB, Redis), a SQLite file, or an AWS Athena account. It has a name, engine, address or file, and options such as SSL and an SSH tunnel. There is no limit on how many you can save.
glossary.not: Not the same as an open connection: a saved connection stays in the list whether or not it is currently connected.

glossary.definition: Everything saved about a connection except its secrets: name, engine, host, port, user, database, file path, SSL options, SSH host and user, notes. Kept in VS Code's per-user extension storage.
glossary.not: Does not include passwords, SSH secrets or AWS secret keys; those are in secret storage.

glossary.definition: A saved connection that is currently connected, shown with the connected icon. It opens when first needed and stays open until closed, *Stop All Connections*, or VS Code shuts down.

VS Code's encrypted store for secrets, backed by the operating system's keychain. Every password, SSH password, key passphrase, AWS secret key and AI provider key the extension keeps is stored here, filed under its connection or provider.
glossary.not: Not the extension's ordinary storage, which holds connection settings unencrypted.

glossary.definition: A way to reach a database that is only visible from another server: the extension signs in to that SSH server and forwards a port on your machine to the database through it.
The default SSH sign-in method: try the SSH agent, then a key (the file you chose, or your default SSH key if it can be opened), then the password.
A single line describing a connection, such as postgresql://user:pass@host:5432/db. The form can connect with it as given, or copy its parts into the separate fields with *Use*.
glossary.not: Not stored in secret storage as a whole; a password kept in the separate password field is.

glossary.definition: A file holding your saved connections so they can be moved to another machine or shared. The default kind has no passwords and strips them from connection strings; it does include notes.
An export that includes passwords and SSH secrets, sealed with a passphrase you choose. Importing it asks for the passphrase; without it the file cannot be opened.
glossary.not: Not the plain-text export, which includes the same passwords readable by anyone.

glossary.definition: How import decides a connection is one you already have: same engine, host, port, database and user (the file for SQLite, the database number for Redis), even if the name differs or one was saved as a connection string.
Optional free text on a connection, up to 2,000 characters, shown when you hover it in the tree. Stored unencrypted and included in every export.
glossary.not: Not a place for passwords; the form says so.

glossary.definition: The stop button at the top of the Connections view. It closes every open connection, tunnel and attempt still in progress, and collapses the tree.
glossary.not: Not *Close Connection*, which closes one.

glossary.definition: Removes every saved connection, every stored secret, every saved query file and all AI settings, keys and usage. The way to leave nothing behind before uninstalling.
A number stamped on every saved connection so that older saved connections can be upgraded safely when the saved format changes. It is 1 today; records without it are treated as older ones.
The piece of the extension that knows how to talk to one kind of database. Each engine has exactly one, and everything else talks only to drivers through the same shared interface.
glossary.not: Not the third-party client library underneath it (pg, mysql2, sql.js, ioredis, the AWS SDK); the driver wraps that library.

glossary.definition: The single shape every engine returns its rows in: column names, rows, a message, and optional extras such as paging, editability, time to live or bytes scanned.
glossary.not: Not engine-specific; an engine adds an optional field rather than inventing its own result.

glossary.definition: The list of names that locates a node in the connections tree, such as database, schema, table. Only the driver that produced it knows what each position means.
glossary.not: Not a file path, and not the same shape on every engine: Athena puts the catalog first and SQLite has no database level.

glossary.definition: A named group of tables inside a database. PostgreSQL shows schemas as their own level; in MySQL a database and a schema are the same thing.
glossary.not: Not the table structure itself; that is shown by View DDL / Structure.

glossary.definition: Opening a table, view or Redis key in the grid to see its first rows or elements, with paging, sort and filters done by the database.
glossary.not: Not running your own SQL; a preview builds its own bounded SELECT, which is shown in the editor.

glossary.definition: The CREATE statement that describes a table's columns and keys. Some engines return their own text; others rebuild it and label it approximate.
Redis's way of listing keys a small batch at a time, optionally keeping only keys that match a pattern. The extension uses it for the key list and key search.
glossary.not: Not KEYS, which lists everything in one blocking call.

glossary.definition: What you type in Search Keys. Plain text matches anywhere in the key name; text with an asterisk, question mark or square brackets is used as a Redis glob exactly as typed.
How long a Redis key has left before Redis deletes it. Keys without one never expire.
A build of SQLite compiled to WebAssembly, so it runs inside VS Code without compiling anything for your machine. It works on an in-memory copy of the file.
glossary.not: Not a live connection to the file: changes reach disk only when the extension writes the whole file back.

glossary.definition: An Athena setting group that every query runs in. It can fix where results are stored and set limits; the extension uses the connection's workgroup, or primary if none is set.
How much data Athena read to answer a query. Athena bills by this amount, so the results footer shows it next to the elapsed time.
An Athena column the data is split by (for example a date). Filtering on it decides whether a query reads one slice or the whole data lake, so the tree and autocomplete flag it.
The top level of the Athena tree: a container of databases. Queries are not run against it; they run against a database inside it.
Wrapping a table, schema or column name in the engine's quote characters, with any quote inside the name doubled, so an unusual name can never be read as SQL.
glossary.not: Not how values are protected; values are always sent separately as parameters.

glossary.definition: The editor tab where you type SQL or a Redis command, run it, and see the results grid below. Each *New Query* or *Preview Rows* opens its own panel; saved files run into one reusable results panel per connection.
glossary.not: Not VS Code's normal text editor, which is where saved query files open.

glossary.definition: The table under the editor that shows returned rows, with typed headers, sorting, per-column filters, a search box, row numbers and, where allowed, editing.
One SQL command, usually ended by a semicolon. Suggestions look only at the statement the caret is in, and the ▶ Run lens in a saved file runs one statement at a time.
glossary.not: The panel's Run sends the highlighted text or the whole editor, which may hold several statements.

glossary.definition: With text highlighted in the editor, Run and Ctrl/Cmd+Enter send only that text; with nothing highlighted, the whole editor runs.

The red button beside Run while a query is in flight, also on Esc. On PostgreSQL and MySQL it stops the query on the server; on Redis it is labelled *Stop waiting* because the server may keep going; SQLite has none.
The dropdown of tables, columns, keywords, functions and types that follows typing in the query panel, and VS Code's own suggestion list in saved query files.
The flavour of SQL an engine speaks: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, or Trino for Athena. It decides which keywords and functions are suggested and how *Format* lays out a statement. Redis has none.
The table and column names an engine reports for suggestions, grouped by table, with a flag when a size limit cut the list short.

Rewrites the statement with consistent line breaks, indentation and upper-case keywords for the connection's dialect. If the statement cannot be read, the text is left exactly as typed and the error is reported.
A .sql file kept in the extension's storage under a database's *Query* node in the tree, opened in VS Code's own editor.
glossary.not: Not a file in your project folder, and not shared between machines.

glossary.definition: The small ▶ Run and { } JSON links VS Code shows above each statement of a saved query file. Run shows results in the grid; JSON opens the rows as a JSON document.

A toggle beside Run that makes one query panel read-only: no queries run and no grid edits, row adds, deletes or TTL changes. It turns on by itself when the AI writes SQL that changes data or schema, and one click turns it off.
glossary.not: Not a database lock and not related to saved query files; it belongs to one open panel and is forgotten when that panel closes.

glossary.definition: Saves the last result to a CSV or JSON file you choose, with only the visible columns, and reports how many rows and columns it wrote.
Copies the checked rows, or every row in view, to the clipboard as JSON in the grid's current order and filters.
The *Columns ▾* button that shows or hides result columns. It reads *Columns 5/9* whenever something is hidden.
The dialog a JSON cell opens into: a collapsible tree with copy buttons and a filter, and a *Raw* tab where the value can be edited.
A query panel opened on a table from the tree. It pages 100 rows at a time, filters and sorts in the database, shows foreign-key links, and is editable when the table has a primary key.
glossary.not: Not the same as typing SELECT * yourself, which returns everything at once and has no paging.

glossary.definition: A result the grid lets you change, because the extension knows its single source table and that table's primary key, and every primary-key column is in the result.
The grid paints at most 2,000 rows and says how many more it is holding; search, sort, export and copy still use every row.
The label in the query panel's toolbar naming the database its queries run against; its tooltip names the connection and repeats the connection's notes.
Following a foreign-key value in a table preview to a new panel showing the matching row of the referenced table.
The AI service the user's requests go to: Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, a local Ollama, or any OpenAI-compatible endpoint they name.
glossary.not: Not a database engine; the extension's database drivers are a separate thing.

glossary.definition: A ready-made provider entry that fills in the base URL, a default model, whether a key is needed and how its models are priced.
glossary.not: Not a model list; the model is free text and the live list is fetched.

glossary.definition: The specific AI model a provider runs a request on. The extension records the name the server reports, which is often more specific than the one chosen.
The user's own secret for their AI provider, pasted once in Settings and kept in the operating system's keychain, one per provider.
glossary.not: Not an admin or billing key; the extension never asks for one.

glossary.definition: The AI assistant runs on the user's own provider account and key; requests go straight from their machine and they pay their provider directly.
glossary.not: Not a subscription or a proxy run by us.

glossary.definition: The strip above a query panel's editor with the request box and the Generate, Explain and Fix buttons. It appears only when a provider is set up and AI is on for that connection.
The three AI actions: write SQL from a request, explain a statement in plain words, or correct a statement that failed using its error.
The compact description of the connected database sent with a request: table and column names, column types where known, and foreign-key links.
glossary.not: Never row data or query results.

glossary.definition: The note on the assist bar saying the schema sent was cut down to a number of tables because the whole schema did not fit.
The one-time question before the first request to a remote provider, naming what will be sent. It can be revoked in Settings; local endpoints skip it.
A checkbox per connection in Settings; unticked, that connection gets no assist bar and every AI request for it is refused.
The unit AI providers count and charge by. Each reply reports exactly how many went in and came out, and the usage tables use those figures.
One line in the local usage ledger for one AI call: when, which provider and model, which action, and the exact token counts.
All usage records, kept only on the user's machine, capped at 5,000 with running totals so all-time figures stay exact.
The read-only list of prices per million tokens, one row per provider and model, each fetched from the provider or LiteLLM and labelled with its source and age. Every cost estimate reads it.
glossary.not: Not the LiteLLM price list itself, which only feeds it.

glossary.definition: An open-source project whose community price file on GitHub prices thousands of models; used for providers, like OpenAI and Anthropic, that publish no prices through their API.
glossary.not: A labelled third-party source, not the provider's own word.

aliases: local copy of the LiteLLM price list
glossary.definition: A trimmed copy of the LiteLLM price file kept on the user's machine so prices work offline; fetched once when first needed and re-downloaded only on request.
A price row's status when it was last fetched more than 30 days ago or its source could not be reached; it still prices calls, but says its age.
Exact token counts times the current price table, worked out on the user's machine. Shown with a ~ and as '—' when no price is known.
glossary.not: Not the provider's bill or account balance.

glossary.definition: The x.y.z version scheme: patch for fixes and small changes, minor for features, major for breaking changes. Every change bumps at least the patch number.
The top section of the changelog where notes collect while work is in progress; a release renames it to the new version and date.
The single installable package file for a VS Code extension. One is built per release and sent to both registries.
Microsoft's extension registry that official VS Code installs from, where the extension is published as brianlab.open-database-client.
The open extension registry that Cursor, VSCodium and Gitpod install from, separate from the Marketplace.
Open VSX's manual approval that the publisher name belongs to us. Until approved, uploads under a name that is also a Marketplace publisher stay stored but invisible.
The git tag the release command creates for each version; pushed only after a successful publish.
Node's built-in test runner, which the project's unit tests use instead of a test framework.
An open-source scanner for secrets in git repositories; run on every commit here.
A script git runs before recording a commit; here it formats staged files and runs the secret scan.

decisions.title: No limit on the number of connections
decisions.decision: Any number of connections can be saved and opened. Nothing in the code counts them.
decisions.why: The extension exists because another database client charges for more than three connections; a free replacement with no cap is the whole point.

decisions.title: Secrets go only to the system keychain
decisions.decision: Database passwords, SSH passwords and passphrases, and AWS secret keys are saved in VS Code's secret storage, filed by connection. The saved connection settings carry none of them.
decisions.why: Connection settings sit in an unencrypted file on disk; the keychain is encrypted and managed by the operating system. It is a house rule for a tool that holds production credentials.

decisions.title: Engines are handed their secrets; they never fetch them
decisions.decision: The connection manager reads secrets from the keychain and passes them to the engine when it connects. Engine code never touches the keychain or any VS Code feature.
decisions.why: Athena's key mode needs two secrets, so connect takes a bundle of secrets rather than one password, and keeping engines free of VS Code keeps them testable and swappable.

decisions.title: Saved connections carry a schema version
decisions.decision: Every save stamps the current schema version (1). Older records are upgraded when read; an SSL connection from before versioning keeps accepting its certificate as it did. Adding an optional field needs no version bump.
decisions.why: A later format change must not silently change how an existing, working connection behaves; switching certificate checks on under an old connection would break it.

decisions.title: Saved field and keychain names are frozen
decisions.decision: The names of saved Athena fields and their keychain entries may not be renamed, retyped or dropped. A field may leave the form while still being read.
decisions.why: Connections already saved on users' machines are read back by those exact names; renaming one silently orphans a saved connection.

decisions.title: Only pure JavaScript drivers, no native modules
decisions.decision: Engines use pure JavaScript libraries and SQLite runs as WebAssembly; optional native speed-ups are left out of the bundle.
decisions.why: Native modules break when VS Code updates its runtime, which would mean a rebuild after every update for a one-person project.

decisions.title: Editing a connection keeps its place
decisions.decision: Saving an existing connection replaces it where it is; only new connections are added at the end.
decisions.why: Users drag connections into an order that means something, and appending on every edit quietly threw that away.

decisions.title: A stuck connection must never need a VS Code restart
decisions.decision: Attempts still in progress are tracked, so *Stop All Connections* and shutdown can close them; the tunnel open and tree loading get hard time limits.
decisions.why: An attempt that hung lived nowhere the clean-up could reach, so a frozen spinner used to mean restarting VS Code.

decisions.title: SSH Auto also tries your default SSH key
decisions.decision: With *Auto* and no key file chosen, the first default SSH key that opens with the given passphrase is offered, after the agent and before the password.
decisions.why: Connections that worked in a terminal failed here, because the SSH library never reads default keys the way the command-line tool does.

decisions.title: The default export carries no passwords, even inside connection strings
decisions.decision: The default export leaves out every stored secret and strips the password from any connection string, flagging those entries. The username is kept.
decisions.why: A file in Downloads is assumed to end up in cloud backup, a chat or a repository; leaving out keychain values alone would still leak passwords written into connection strings. A username is not a secret and is already stored in the clear elsewhere.

decisions.title: One export command with three choices, safest first
decisions.decision: Export is a single command whose picker offers without passwords, encrypted, and plain text behind a confirmation, each with its cost stated.
decisions.why: Three separate export entries in a small menu would have buried the safe one; a picker shows the trade-off at the moment of choosing. This replaced the blueprint's two-command plan.

decisions.title: Encrypted exports use scrypt and AES-256-GCM
decisions.decision: The passphrase is stretched with scrypt and the file sealed with AES-256-GCM, with a fresh salt and IV per file and the seal checked on open.
decisions.why: Uses Node's built-in crypto, so no new dependency, and a tampered file fails loudly instead of decrypting to garbage.

decisions.title: Import only ever adds
decisions.decision: Import appends new connections, skips ones already saved, renames a name clash on a different server, and gives every entry a fresh id.
decisions.why: Explicit requirement; re-importing the same file must do nothing, and carrying ids across machines could pair a connection with another one's stored password.

decisions.title: Import files are untrusted and allowlisted
decisions.decision: Import keeps only known fields with the right type and drops everything else, reporting each dropped entry.
decisions.why: Some fields are file paths the extension will later read and others are addresses it will connect to, so an import file is attacker-controllable input.

decisions.title: Notes are plain text, capped, and say so
decisions.decision: Connection notes are an optional field capped at 2,000 characters, stored unencrypted and exported in every mode; the form and the export picker state this plainly instead of scanning for secrets.
decisions.why: A free-text box is where people paste passwords; a scanner would pretend to catch them, while an honest warning at the point of entry can change behaviour.

decisions.title: Reset All Data is best-effort and honest
decisions.decision: Reset tries every step, always clears the saved connections, and tells the user how many keychain entries may remain if any delete failed.
decisions.why: For an irreversible remove-everything action, ending in a consistent state and reporting truthfully matters more than stopping at the first error.

decisions.title: Every engine sits behind one driver interface
decisions.decision: Each database engine is one file implementing a shared interface; the tree, query panel and commands only ever talk to that interface.
decisions.why: It keeps each engine's quirks in one place, so adding or fixing an engine does not ripple through the user interface, and it lets the extension copy the reference client's familiar layout across all engines.

decisions.title: Capabilities only some engines have are optional, never faked
decisions.decision: Cancelling, counting rows and setting expiry are optional on the interface. An engine that cannot do one leaves it out, and the rest of the app checks before using it.
decisions.why: A pretend version lies to the user: a zero row count reads as an empty table, and an Abort button that cannot stop anything is worse than none. On Athena a count would be a full, billed scan.

decisions.title: Pure-JavaScript drivers and WebAssembly SQLite, no native modules
decisions.decision: PostgreSQL, MySQL and Redis use pure-JavaScript client libraries, and SQLite uses its WebAssembly build.
decisions.why: Native modules break when VS Code updates its runtime and must be rebuilt; avoiding them removes that recurring cost for a one-person project.

decisions.title: PostgreSQL browses the whole server with one pool per database
decisions.decision: A PostgreSQL connection lists every database on the server and opens a separate small pool for each one when it is first used.
decisions.why: A PostgreSQL session is bound to one database, so browsing and editing tables in others needs its own connections; opening them lazily avoids connecting to databases nobody opens.

decisions.title: Redis keys are listed with SCAN, capped at 500
decisions.decision: The key list and key search walk the keyspace in batches with SCAN and a server-side match pattern, stopping at 500 keys and saying so.
decisions.why: A real database holds hundreds of keys or more and a flat unsorted list was unusable. Batches keep a large keyspace from stalling the server or the tree, and the cap keeps the tree readable.

decisions.title: Table search filters in the tree; key search filters on the server
decisions.decision: Searching tables narrows the already-loaded list inside the tree, while searching Redis keys sends the pattern to Redis.
decisions.why: Table lists are small, so filtering locally is instant and needs no query per keystroke; a Redis database can hold far more keys than the tree lists, so only the server can search all of them.

decisions.title: Athena is a small driver on the AWS SDK, rebuilt from scratch
decisions.decision: Athena support is one driver file, one registry case and one form section using the official AWS SDK, replacing an earlier branch roughly ten times larger.
decisions.why: The earlier branch invented its own cancellation layer that clashed with the one already on main and touched every driver; porting the few hundred lines that carry the feature was cheaper than reconciling two designs.

refs.label: Athena blueprint: rebase vs reset, scope

decisions.title: Clicking an Athena table does not preview it
decisions.decision: On Athena a click only expands a table; previewing is an explicit Preview Rows action that runs one capped statement and does not page.
decisions.why: Every preview is a billed query that can scan a terabyte-scale table, so a stray click or a next-page click must not spend money.

decisions.title: Athena browsing uses free catalog lookups, never queries
decisions.decision: The tree, autocomplete, column details and DDL for Athena come from its metadata APIs, never from querying its information schema.
decisions.why: Querying the information schema is billed like any other query; the metadata APIs scan nothing.

decisions.title: Athena shows bytes scanned, not a dollar estimate
decisions.decision: The results footer reports how much data a query scanned, without converting it to money.
decisions.why: A per-region price table goes stale silently and is wrong for reserved capacity, while the scanned amount comes free with every response.

decisions.title: SQLite shows no Abort button
decisions.decision: The SQLite driver offers no way to cancel, and the query panel hides Abort for it.
decisions.why: The WebAssembly engine runs on the extension's main thread, so while a statement runs nothing can even deliver a cancel; a button there would be a lie.

decisions.title: Every limit says so when it cuts something off
