decisions.decision: Wherever the extension shows less than everything (500 keys, 200 list elements, Athena's capped rows, 300 Athena tables, autocomplete caps), it says so in the tree or grid.
decisions.why: A cut the user cannot see makes a 5,000-element list look like a 200-element one; the project treats hidden truncation as the one thing it is not allowed to do.

refs.label: CLAUDE.md Conventions: be honest in UX

decisions.title: Autocomplete is a custom widget inside the panel
decisions.decision: Suggestions are drawn by the panel itself over its plain editor, rather than bundling a full code editor or sending SQL editing to .sql files.
decisions.why: A bundled editor would add megabytes to an extension sold as lightweight, and moving typing to a separate file would change where people write queries.

decisions.title: One formatting library serves both formatting and suggestions
decisions.decision: The extension takes a single SQL formatting library, loaded one dialect at a time, and reads its dialect word lists for suggestions too.
decisions.why: Loaded per dialect it adds about 87 KB, and its word lists give hundreds of real functions per engine instead of 46 shared hand-written keywords.

decisions.title: Suggestion reasoning runs in the extension, not the panel
decisions.decision: The panel sends the text before the caret and only draws the reply; all the reasoning lives in tested code in the extension.
decisions.why: Keeping it there means it is covered by unit tests instead of being duplicated as untested panel script.

decisions.title: Suggestions read the statement backwards instead of parsing it
decisions.decision: Context comes from a backward scan of words (FROM, JOIN, aliases, dots), not a full SQL parser; common table expressions and subqueries are not understood.
decisions.why: The scan is enough for the reference behaviour and avoids a parser dependency; revisit only if it measurably fails.

decisions.title: Highlighted text is what runs
decisions.decision: With a non-blank selection only the selection runs, and the Run button follows the same rule as Ctrl/Cmd+Enter.
decisions.why: One rule to learn rather than two, and the status line says *Running selection…* so it is never ambiguous.

decisions.title: Abort really stops the query on PostgreSQL and MySQL
decisions.decision: Typed queries run on a dedicated connection so Abort can ask the server to stop that statement, rather than only stopping the spinner.
decisions.why: Users point this at shared production databases; a button that only hides the wait would leave the query running there.

decisions.title: SQLite gets no Abort button, Redis gets Stop waiting
decisions.decision: Engines that cannot cancel do not show a fake Abort: SQLite shows none, and Redis says *Stop waiting* and that the server may still be working.
decisions.why: SQLite's engine runs inside the extension and blocks it while working, so a click could not even arrive; honesty outranks a uniform toolbar.

decisions.title: One query in flight per panel
decisions.decision: Run is unavailable while a query is running, and results from an aborted run are dropped.
decisions.why: A second run would orphan the first and leave Abort pointing at the wrong statement; cancellation is a race the panel must win honestly.

decisions.title: The query lock blocks editing as well as running
decisions.decision: A locked panel refuses runs and every grid change: cell edits, adding and deleting rows, and TTL changes.
decisions.why: A lock that only blocked Run would still let an unreviewed write happen through the grid.

decisions.title: One click unlocks, with no confirmation
decisions.decision: Unlocking is a single click, whether the lock was set by hand or by the AI.
decisions.why: The deliberate click is the safety; a confirmation on top was judged friction without added safety.

decisions.title: Only AI-written writes lock the panel automatically
decisions.decision: Generate and Fix results that change data or schema engage the lock; SQL the developer typed never does, and over-locking on a false match is accepted.
decisions.why: AI SQL lands selected, one keystroke from running, which is exactly how an accidental update happens; a hand-typed write was written on purpose.

decisions.title: JSON is detected by the value, not the column type
decisions.decision: Any cell holding a JSON object or array, or text that reads as one, gets the viewer, on any result.
decisions.why: Column types are only known for table previews, and SQLite and Redis keep JSON as plain text, so a type check would miss most cases.

decisions.title: JSON is edited on the Raw tab only
decisions.decision: The tree is read-only in this version; Save works only on *Raw*.
decisions.why: Keeps the first version small and keeps the existing save path unchanged.

decisions.title: Hidden columns are not remembered after the panel closes
decisions.decision: Column choices last only while the panel is open, and are not stored per table.
decisions.why: Remembering them properly needs its own decision on the key, the storage and when a schema change invalidates it; recorded so the omission reads as a choice.

decisions.title: Export writes only the visible columns and says so
decisions.decision: Export and Copy follow the column picker, and the confirmation reports how many columns were kept.
decisions.why: A silently narrower file is the failure mode; the export should match what was on screen and admit it.

decisions.title: The add-row form ignores hidden columns
decisions.decision: *＋ Row* always lists every column, hidden or not.
decisions.why: It is a data-entry form; leaving out a required column would fail the insert for a reason the user cannot see.

decisions.title: The grid paints at most 2,000 rows
decisions.decision: Only the first 2,000 matching rows are drawn, with a note naming the full count; select-all means the painted rows.
decisions.why: Painting 50,000 rows built about 40 MB of page and froze the window; select-all limited to painted rows keeps Delete from reaching rows never shown.

decisions.title: A panel is bound to one database and shows it
decisions.decision: A panel opened from a table preview runs against the database the table came from, and the toolbar badge names it; the schema is deliberately not shown.
decisions.why: Panels used to run against the connection's default database and fail with *relation does not exist* on multi-database servers; queries are not pinned to a schema.

decisions.title: Saved queries are real files, edited in VS Code's editor
decisions.decision: Saved queries are plain .sql files in the extension's storage folder, opened in VS Code's own editor rather than stored as records.
decisions.why: As ordinary files, VS Code handles editing, saving and undo, and its native suggestions, formatting and lenses can be added on top.

decisions.title: The search box covers the loaded page and says so
decisions.decision: On a paged preview the global search filters only the loaded page, and the placeholder and scope line say so; column filters still search the whole table in the database.
decisions.why: True table-wide search means an unindexed match across every column, rejected for cost; silently missing rows was the bug being fixed.

decisions.title: The AI assistant is bring-your-own-key
decisions.decision: Users connect their own provider account and key; there is no hosted proxy, no billing of ours and no telemetry of prompts.
decisions.why: It costs us nothing to run, keeps a third party from sitting between the user and their key, and hosted AI database tools have already disappeared, so it is also the durable choice.

decisions.title: Two hand-written adapters behind one provider interface, no SDKs
decisions.decision: Every provider is reached through one interface with exactly two adapters, Anthropic and OpenAI-compatible; presets are data and the model is free text.
decisions.why: Two wire formats cover the whole market, local models included; vendor libraries would add hundreds of kilobytes to a tool sold as lightweight for what is one request each, and it follows the same one-interface rule the database engines use.

decisions.title: AI-written SQL is never run automatically
decisions.decision: Generated SQL is placed in the editor selected; running it is always the user's click. Destructive shapes get a warning, and writes lock the editor.
decisions.why: Wrong SQL that looks right, or destructive SQL, is the main risk of the feature; showing it for review and keeping the run a human step is the mitigation.

decisions.title: Schema goes to the AI, row data never does
decisions.decision: Requests carry the prompt, schema names and types, foreign-key links and the dialect; never row data, query results, credentials or connection hosts.
decisions.why: Described as a privacy line, not a scope cut: users point this at strangers' production and regulated databases.

decisions.title: Send the full schema with relations, and say when it is trimmed
decisions.decision: The context is the whole schema plus foreign keys; over a budget it is cut to the tables the request names and their neighbours, and the assist bar says so.
decisions.why: Answers need the real joins, and a wrong answer caused by missing context must be something the user can diagnose.

decisions.title: Ask for consent once; local endpoints skip it
decisions.decision: A native modal before the first request to a remote provider names what will be sent; accepted once, revocable in Settings. Localhost endpoints skip it.
decisions.why: AI calls are the extension's first traffic to the internet, so sharing must be explicit; with a local model nothing leaves the machine.

decisions.title: AI can be switched off per connection
decisions.decision: Each connection has its own AI checkbox; off means no assist bar and refused requests, applied to panels already open.
decisions.why: For regulated databases (PDPA, data sovereignty) the user must be able to keep schema names away from any provider. The 1.4.2 fix made it reach open panels because that screen's whole purpose is keeping a regulated database away from the model.

decisions.title: The AI assistant is SQL-only; Redis is out
decisions.decision: Redis panels never get the assist bar, and Redis command generation is not planned.
decisions.why: What AI adds to SQL (joins, grouping, dialect, recalling the schema) has no Redis counterpart; Redis work here runs through the tree, not the command box.

decisions.title: No price ships with the extension
decisions.decision: Every price is fetched, from the provider's own model list or the LiteLLM community list, labelled with its source, and read-only.
decisions.why: The original hand-seeded prices had already drifted (one model at half its real price); the directive was that every value must be true.

decisions.title: Costs are computed when shown, not stored
decisions.decision: The ledger stores exact token counts only; cost is tokens times the current price table every time it is displayed.
decisions.why: A model with no price can then honestly show '—' instead of a frozen $0; the accepted consequence is that history is re-costed at today's prices.

decisions.title: No account balance or credits in the extension
decisions.decision: The usage view shows local estimates and sends users to their provider's dashboard for real billing.
decisions.why: Provider billing APIs need separate admin keys most users do not have and should not paste into an editor extension.

decisions.title: A model is priced on its first real call
decisions.decision: When a call is recorded for a model with no price row, a row is filed under the model name the server reported; removing it with ✕ lasts only until the next use.
decisions.why: Servers report more specific names than the one requested, so pricing the requested name would file it where the ledger never looks; pricing on use also limits rows to models that cost money.

decisions.title: Keep the whole LiteLLM list locally; refresh only on request
decisions.decision: The full LiteLLM price list is stored trimmed on the user's machine, fetched once when empty and otherwise only when the user presses Update.
decisions.why: An in-memory copy vanished with the window, failed offline and covered two providers; a 1.6 MB download nobody asked for is not acceptable on opening Settings, so age is shown instead.

decisions.title: Custom endpoints are priced only against a provider the user names
decisions.decision: A custom endpoint gets LiteLLM prices only from the LiteLLM provider the user types; blank means no prices.
decisions.why: Matching by model name across every provider would price a local model off an unrelated cloud host's row, a made-up number shown as real.

decisions.title: Bump the version for every change
decisions.decision: Every change, however small, gets at least a patch bump; numbers are never reused or skipped, and the version and changelog move together.
decisions.why: Recorded as strict house policy; the registries refuse a reused number anyway, and a version with no changelog section cannot be published.

decisions.title: The changelog is stamped by the version bump itself
decisions.decision: The npm version hook moves the Unreleased notes into a dated section for the new number, so bumping and stamping cannot be done apart.
decisions.why: Bumping any other way (for example the Marketplace tool's own bump) would break the lock-step between version and changelog.

refs.label: Publishing: do not use vsce bump

decisions.title: Releasing stays local; publishing pushes
decisions.decision: The release command commits, tags and packages without pushing; the publish script pushes the commit and tags only after a successful publish.
decisions.why: Until publish a bad release can still be undone locally; once the version is public the tag must not stay local.

decisions.title: One package file goes to both registries
decisions.decision: The publish scripts build the package once and upload that exact file to the Marketplace and to Open VSX, checking the Open VSX credential before anything is published.
decisions.why: Letting each registry's tool package on its own produced two builds of the same version; checking first avoids the two registries ending on different versions.

decisions.title: Report an inactive Open VSX upload as such
decisions.decision: The status check looks up the namespace and says 'not live, namespace not verified' instead of 'not published'; the Open VSX publish warns before uploading into an unverified namespace.
decisions.why: Open VSX returns the same not-found for an inactive upload as for a missing one, which made a successful upload look like a failure.

decisions.title: A failed GitHub release does not fail the publish
decisions.decision: After pushing, the publish script creates the GitHub release with notes from the changelog; if that fails it only warns.
decisions.why: By then the Marketplace has the version and the tag is pushed, so a non-zero exit would report a failed publish that actually succeeded.

decisions.title: Unit tests cover pure logic over the compiled output
decisions.decision: Tests are plain Node test files that load the compiled modules; anything tested must be exported and must not need the editor.
decisions.why: No extension-host harness is needed and tests run in seconds; the cost is that editor behaviour is checked by hand.

decisions.title: Scan history and the staged change on every commit
decisions.decision: The pre-commit hook runs gitleaks twice, over all branches' history and over the staged change, redacted, and refuses to commit without gitleaks.
decisions.why: A history scan cannot see what is not committed yet, and an unscanned commit is worse than a blocked one.

decisions.title: The Open VSX token is read only from the environment
decisions.decision: The Open VSX credential is loaded into an environment variable with a hidden prompt and never passed on a command line or kept in a file.
decisions.why: On a command line it would land in shell history and process listings.

dangerZones.title: Renaming a saved field or keychain name orphans connections
dangerZones.risk: Saved connections and their secrets are read back by exact names. Renaming, retyping or dropping one silently disconnects existing users' connections from their settings or passwords.
dangerZones.guidance: Treat saved field names and keychain entry names as frozen. Remove a field from the form if needed, but keep reading it, and carry it through edits.

dangerZones.title: A new secret must be wired everywhere secrets go
dangerZones.risk: A secret is handled in several places: saving, connecting, deleting, Reset All Data, the export with passwords, and import. Missing one leaves a password behind, loses it on transfer, or produces a connection that cannot sign in.
dangerZones.guidance: Give a new secret its own keychain entry, then add it to save, delete, reset, the secrets list used by export and import, and the import merge, and test the round trip.

dangerZones.title: A new connection field is lost on import unless it is allowlisted
dangerZones.risk: Export copies every field automatically, but import keeps only listed fields. A new field leaves in the export and is silently dropped when the file is imported.
dangerZones.guidance: When adding a connection field, add it to the import allowlist with its type and cover the export-import round trip in the portability tests.

dangerZones.title: A time limit stops the waiting, not the work
dangerZones.risk: When a time limit fires, the connection attempt keeps running in the background. Code that assumes a timed-out attempt is gone can leak a tunnel or a half-open connection.
dangerZones.guidance: After a time limit, tear down what was built, as the connection manager's failure path does.

dangerZones.title: Names built into SQL must always be quoted
dangerZones.risk: Values are sent separately and are safe, but table, schema and column names are pasted into the generated SQL. A name built in without quoting can break the statement or be read as extra SQL.
dangerZones.guidance: Route every generated name through the shared quoting helpers (double quotes for PostgreSQL and SQLite, backticks for MySQL), or Athena's own pair, which differ between its query and DDL dialects. Keep values as parameters. Extend the quoting tests when adding a call site. One SQLite foreign-key lookup currently bypasses the helper and is worth fixing.

dangerZones.title: SQLite rewrites the whole file on every change
dangerZones.risk: The file is copied into memory at connect, and each change writes the whole copy back. Edits made by another program in between are silently overwritten, and a multi-statement run that begins with SELECT changes memory without writing the file.
dangerZones.guidance: Treat the connection as the only writer of that file while it is open. If you change when writes happen, keep every modifying path persisting, and reconsider the starts-with-SELECT test. The blueprint still says read-only, and promoting the write-back caveat into the in-app guide is an open task.

dangerZones.title: On Athena, ordinary clicks can cost money
dangerZones.risk: Every Athena statement is billed by data scanned, including cancelled ones. A change that previews on click, adds server-side paging, counts rows, queries the information schema or cancels on close would spend the user's money without asking.
dangerZones.guidance: Keep tree, autocomplete and DDL on metadata APIs; keep previews as one explicit, capped statement; never add a row count; leave dispose without cancel. Show bytes scanned on every outcome.

dangerZones.title: Claiming a capability the engine does not have
dangerZones.risk: Callers trust the optional driver members. A stub that returns zero rows reads as an empty table and breaks paging; claiming a real cancel on an engine that only stops waiting tells the user the server stopped when it did not.
dangerZones.guidance: Omit optional members the engine cannot honour, set the cancel flag true only when the server really stops, and guard every optional call. Note that the Redis driver still returns a zero row count, against the interface's own advice.

dangerZones.title: Redis reads can be heavy on big databases or big keys
dangerZones.risk: Listing is batched and capped, but a raw KEYS command typed by the user still runs on the server even after Stop waiting, and hash and set previews read the whole value with no cap.
dangerZones.guidance: Keep key listing on batched SCAN with its caps and round-trip budgets. Do not swap in KEYS. If you touch hash or set previews, consider a cap with the same visible notice lists and sorted sets use.

dangerZones.title: Grid editing depends on knowing the row's primary key
dangerZones.risk: Every edit and delete finds its row by primary key alone. Offering editing on a result whose source table or key is uncertain, such as a join, a view, or a table without a key, could change or delete the wrong rows.
dangerZones.guidance: Keep results read-only whenever the single source table and its full primary key are not certain; do not add a fallback that matches rows on their other values.

refs.label: parseFromTable: fall back to read-only rather than guess

dangerZones.title: The panel's strict content rules
dangerZones.risk: The panel is one self-contained page that may only run its own nonce-stamped inline script; anything loaded from outside, or an inline event attribute, simply does not run.
dangerZones.guidance: Keep the page self-contained, add behaviour inside the existing script, and route anything needing a native VS Code prompt through the extension side.

dangerZones.title: Every run path must carry its run number
dangerZones.risk: Cancelling is a race, and one engine connection serves every panel on it. A run without its own number can paint a result the user aborted, or cancel another panel's query.
dangerZones.guidance: Any new way to start a typed query must tag it with the panel's run token and echo the run number back, so stale results are dropped and cancels hit only that run.

dangerZones.title: The query lock is enforced at a handful of panel checkpoints
dangerZones.risk: The lock is checked inside the panel at each run and grid-edit entry point. A new action that writes data without the same check silently weakens read-only.
dangerZones.guidance: Any new grid or run action must check the lock first and show the standard lock message.

dangerZones.title: Typing in the query panel must never open a connection
dangerZones.risk: If the suggestion path connected on demand, a keystroke could trigger a connection, an SSH tunnel or a password prompt as a side effect.
dangerZones.guidance: Load schema names in the panel only when the connection is already live, and fall back to the dialect vocabulary otherwise.

dangerZones.title: What leaves the machine when AI is used
dangerZones.risk: AI requests are the extension's only traffic to the internet. They carry the typed request, the query in the editor, earlier requests in that panel, a failed statement's error for Fix, schema names, column types and foreign-key links, and the dialect, to whichever host the user configured. Adding anything to a prompt changes what a user's consent covered.
dangerZones.guidance: Keep row data, results, passwords and hosts out of every prompt. Any new prompt content must also appear in the consent wording and the AI & your data guide in the same change. Keep the controls working: the consent question before the first remote request, Revoke, the per-connection checkbox, and the trim notice.

dangerZones.title: AI-written SQL can be wrong or destructive
dangerZones.risk: A model can return SQL that looks right but is wrong, or that drops, truncates or rewrites data. A change that runs AI output automatically, or weakens the warning or the lock, puts real databases at risk.
dangerZones.guidance: Never run AI output without the user's click. Keep the destructive warning and the automatic lock on writes; the token scans deliberately over-trigger, so do not narrow them to save a click.

dangerZones.title: Cost figures are only as current as the price table
dangerZones.risk: Estimates use fetched list prices that age, and history is re-costed at today's prices, so a refresh can change past months. Hand-seeded prices drifted before (one model shown at half its price).
dangerZones.guidance: Never ship or hardcode a price. Keep every figure labelled as an estimate, keep the stale status visible, and show '—' rather than $0 when nothing prices a model.

dangerZones.title: Anything newly stored must be measured and purged
dangerZones.risk: Settings promises to measure everything the extension keeps and Reset all data promises to remove it. A new stored key that is not added to both quietly breaks both promises.
dangerZones.guidance: When adding stored state, register it in the storage usage list and in the matching delete-everything routine in the same change.

dangerZones.title: Never skip or reuse a version number
dangerZones.risk: A registry refuses a number it has seen, and a version bumped outside the release scripts has no changelog section, so publishing fails or the in-app changelog drifts from what shipped.
dangerZones.guidance: Bump only with the release scripts, patch at minimum for every change; never with the Marketplace tool's own bump.

refs.label: Publishing: do not use vsce bump

dangerZones.title: Publishing cannot be taken back
dangerZones.risk: Once a version is on a registry it is public and its number is spent; the push that follows makes the tag public too.
dangerZones.guidance: Run the publish with --dry-run first if unsure; until publish, a bad release can be undone locally by deleting the tag and the release commit.

dangerZones.title: Some docs still describe an older extension
dangerZones.risk: Several written records lag the code: the main blueprint still lists SQLite as read-only and the SSH tunnel as out of scope, the manual test guide still says four engines and an old build step, and a comment names a keychain entry the code no longer uses. A newcomer who trusts them builds on something that is no longer true.
dangerZones.guidance: When code and a doc disagree, the code and the task list are current; fix the doc in the same change, and treat the blueprint's module table as history until it is refreshed.

readingOrder.why: The repo's rules in one page: the Driver rule, layout, build and test commands, versioning policy and conventions.
Why the extension exists (no connection cap), the scope, and the pure-JavaScript constraint behind most technical choices.
Every change maps to a task here; each milestone section also records the bug or reason behind it.
The one interface every engine implements and the single result shape the grid reads. Nothing outside the drivers imports an engine library.
Activation and every command in one file, including export, import, Reset All Data and Stop All.
Where connections and their secrets are saved, the schema version, and the reset logic.
How a connection is opened on demand, through the SSH tunnel, and torn down even when it is stuck.

Bundle the extension into dist/extension.js and copy the SQLite WebAssembly file.
Open the folder in VS Code and press F5 (Run Extension). It bundles first, then opens an Extension Development Host window; click the database icon there.
Compile to out/ and run the node:test unit tests (pure logic, no VS Code).

rules.title: Engines only behind the Driver interface
rules.why: The tree, query panel and commands never import an engine library; adding an engine is one driver file plus one registry case, and nothing else should need to know.

rules.title: Secrets only in VS Code secret storage
rules.why: Never log or hardcode credentials; saved connection settings are unencrypted on disk, the keychain is not.

rules.title: Every change maps to a task in docs/task.md
rules.why: The project is spec-driven; tasks carry [SDD][Mx] prefixes and are checked off as they land, with strategy in the blueprint.

rules.title: Bump the version for every change and keep the changelog in step
rules.why: SemVer, patch at minimum, never reuse or skip a number; notes go under Unreleased and the release scripts stamp them.

rules.title: Be honest in the interface
rules.why: Show truncation, limits and failures rather than hiding them; best-effort operations report what they actually did.

rules.title: Commit, push and version bumps only when asked
rules.why: Single-author repo; the author decides when work is recorded and released.

openQuestions.question: Should Test Connection get the same 15-second cap on opening the SSH tunnel that a real connect has?
openQuestions.context: The connection manager wraps the tunnel open in a 15-second limit; the form's Test Connection opens its tunnel directly, bounded only by the SSH handshake timeout (5 s by default, user-editable).
openQuestions.meanwhile: Treat the SSH handshake timeout as the bound for testing.

openQuestions.question: Should Reset All Data also clear the remembered last-seen version, so a reset install behaves like a fresh one?
openQuestions.context: Reset clears connections, secrets, query files and AI data, but the last-seen version key written on activate is left in place.
openQuestions.meanwhile: Assume the version marker survives a reset; nothing reads it for behaviour yet beyond logging.

openQuestions.question: Should an Athena preview read 100 rows or 500?
openQuestions.context: The README and the 1.4.0 changelog say Athena previews read up to 500 rows. The query panel always asks for 100, and the driver takes the smaller number, so previews actually read 100. Its notice then says "Previews read at most 500 rows", which is wrong for what was shown.
openQuestions.meanwhile: The map describes what the code does: 100 rows per Athena preview, with a notice that names the wrong number.

openQuestions.question: Is SQLite write-back finished, or still the open item the blueprint says it is?
openQuestions.context: Blueprint M4 says SQLite is read-only and write-back is the one open item. task.md marks write-back done, and the code rewrites the whole file after any non-SELECT statement or grid edit. Nothing detects another program changing the file in the meantime.
openQuestions.meanwhile: The map treats write-back as shipped, and lists the whole-file overwrite as a danger zone.

openQuestions.question: Should Redis hash and set previews be capped like lists and sorted sets?
openQuestions.context: Lists and sorted sets stop at 200 elements and say so. Hashes and sets are read whole, so a key with millions of members goes to the grid all at once.
openQuestions.meanwhile: Assume hash and set previews are uncapped, and avoid opening very large ones on production servers.

openQuestions.question: Should previewing an Athena table under a non-default catalog work?
openQuestions.context: The tree lists every data catalog. A preview builds a database.table statement with no catalog, and every query runs in the connection's configured catalog, so previewing a table from another catalog would look for it in the wrong catalog.
openQuestions.meanwhile: Treat browsing other catalogs as working and previewing from them as unverified.

openQuestions.question: On MySQL, should a query panel's raw queries actually run against the database named in its badge?
openQuestions.context: The panel binds to a database and the badge names it, and task.md M18.8 lists MySQL as a multi-database engine for that binding. But the MySQL engine ignores the database it is given for typed queries, so unqualified table names resolve against the connection's configured database, while suggestions use the badge's database.
openQuestions.meanwhile: Treat the badge as reliable for PostgreSQL and Redis; on MySQL, qualify table names with the database when it differs from the connection's own.

openQuestions.question: What should Run do when the editor holds several statements?
openQuestions.context: No record decides it. Reading the code, PostgreSQL appears to run them all and return a list of results the grid does not unpack (likely an empty grid with an odd status), MySQL has multiple statements off and should error, and SQLite runs them all but shows the first result set. Highlight-to-run is the documented way to pick one.
openQuestions.meanwhile: Highlight one statement before running, or use the ▶ Run lens in a saved file.

openQuestions.question: When an inline cell save fails, should the grid put the old value back?
openQuestions.context: The grid shows the new value before the database answers. On failure the status line says *Update failed*, but the cell keeps the typed value until a refresh, which can read as saved.
openQuestions.meanwhile: Read the status line after every edit, and refresh when it says the update failed.

openQuestions.question: Should running a saved file into the shared results panel respect that panel's query lock and run counter?
openQuestions.context: The ▶ Run lens and *Run Query File* re-run straight from the extension side into the reusable results panel, so the panel's lock (which lives in the panel) is not consulted. That re-run also carries run number 0, so if someone has already pressed Run inside that panel, its result looks stale to the panel and is dropped. The lock discovery puts tree-side commands out of scope.
openQuestions.meanwhile: Do not rely on a lock in the reusable results panel; if a lens run shows no new rows, close that panel and run again.

openQuestions.question: How will releases be published after Azure DevOps retires global personal access credentials on 1 December 2026?
openQuestions.context: Publishing today uses a vsce login with an Azure DevOps credential. The publishing guide notes global ones are being retired on 1 December 2026, and the task list has an unchecked item to publish from CI on a version tag with repository secrets. There is no CI pipeline in the repo yet.
openQuestions.meanwhile: Keep publishing by hand from a clean tree with the publish scripts.

openQuestions.question: Should each usage record keep the price that applied when the call was made, instead of re-costing history at today's prices?
openQuestions.context: Costs are worked out at display time from the current price table, so refreshing a price changes past periods. The pricing guide calls freezing cost per entry a known possible follow-up.
openQuestions.meanwhile: History is re-costed at today's prices and every figure is labelled an estimate.
